editorial.question: Does your organization test its contingency plan on a schedule, review the results, and take corrective action where the test reveals problems?
editorial.whyItMatters: Untested plans often fail when they are needed, through outdated contacts, missing steps, or backups that will not restore. Testing finds these gaps while the stakes are low.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The contingency plan is tested at the frequency you define using the tests you choose, such as checklists, walk-throughs, tabletop exercises, or simulations, to determine the plan's effectiveness and your readiness to carry it out. Test results are reviewed, and corrective actions are started where needed.
nextSteps: Schedule a tabletop exercise that walks key people through a realistic outage scenario.
Record what worked and what did not.
Assign fixes for the problems found, and update the plan.

requirements.title: Coordinate with Related Plans

statement.text: Coordinate contingency plan testing with organizational elements responsible for related plans.

requirements.discussion: Plans related to contingency planning for organizational systems include Business Continuity Plans, Disaster Recovery Plans, Continuity of Operations Plans, Crisis Communications Plans, Critical Infrastructure Plans, Cyber Incident Response Plans, and Occupant Emergency Plans. Coordination of contingency plan testing does not require organizations to create organizational elements to handle related plans or to align such elements with specific plans. However, it does require that if such organizational elements are responsible for related plans, organizations coordinate with those elements.

objectives.text: contingency plan testing is coordinated with organizational elements responsible for related plans.

editorial.question: Does your organization coordinate contingency plan testing with the people responsible for related plans, such as disaster recovery and incident response?
editorial.whyItMatters: Testing plans separately can miss problems that only appear when teams work together. Coordinated testing shows whether the plans fit together in a real event.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Contingency plan testing is coordinated with the parts of your organization responsible for related plans, where those exist. You are not required to create new teams solely for this purpose.
nextSteps: Identify the owners of related plans.
Invite them to help plan and take part in contingency tests.
Share results so each plan owner can update their plan.

requirements.title: Alternate Processing Site

statement.text: Test the contingency plan at the alternate processing site:

items.label: (a)
items.text: To familiarize contingency personnel with the facility and available resources; and

items.label: (b)
items.text: To evaluate the capabilities of the alternate processing site to support contingency operations.

requirements.discussion: Conditions at the alternate processing site may be significantly different than the conditions at the primary site. Having the opportunity to visit the alternate site and experience the actual capabilities available at the site can provide valuable information on potential vulnerabilities that could affect essential organizational mission and business functions. The on-site visit can also provide an opportunity to refine the contingency plan to address the vulnerabilities discovered during testing.

objectives.label: CP-04(02)(a)
objectives.text: the contingency plan is tested at the alternate processing site to familiarize contingency personnel with the facility and available resources;

objectives.label: CP-04(02)(b)
objectives.text: the contingency plan is tested at the alternate processing site to evaluate the capabilities of the alternate processing site to support contingency operations.

editorial.question: Does your organization test its contingency plan at the alternate processing site, so staff know the facility and its ability to support operations is confirmed?
editorial.whyItMatters: An alternate site can look adequate on paper but differ from your primary site in equipment, space, or connectivity. Testing there reveals gaps before you depend on it.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The contingency plan is tested at the alternate processing site to familiarize contingency personnel with the facility and its available resources, and to evaluate the site's ability to support contingency operations.
nextSteps: Schedule a test at the alternate site with the staff who would work there, or exercise failover if the site is a cloud service.
Walk through recovery steps using the site's actual equipment and connections.
Record gaps, and update the contingency plan or site arrangements.

requirements.title: Automated Testing

statement.text: Test the contingency plan using {{param:cp-04.03_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Automated mechanisms facilitate thorough and effective testing of contingency plans by providing more complete coverage of contingency issues, selecting more realistic test scenarios and environments, and effectively stressing the system and supported mission and business functions.

objectives.text: the contingency plan is tested using {{param:cp-04.03_odp}}.

parameters.label: automated mechanisms
parameters.guidance: automated mechanisms for contingency plan testing are defined;

requirements.title: Full Recovery and Reconstitution

statement.text: Include a full recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state as part of contingency plan testing.

requirements.discussion: Recovery is executing contingency plan activities to restore organizational mission and business functions. Reconstitution takes place following recovery and includes activities for returning systems to fully operational states. Organizations establish a known state for systems that includes system state information for hardware, software programs, and data. Preserving system state information facilitates system restart and return to the operational mode of organizations with less disruption of mission and business processes.

objectives.label: CP-04(04)[01]
objectives.text: a full recovery of the system to a known state is included as part of contingency plan testing;

objectives.label: CP-04(04)[02]
objectives.text: a full reconstitution of the system to a known state is included as part of contingency plan testing.

requirements.title: Self-challenge

statement.text: Employ {{param:cp-04.05_odp.01}} to {{param:cp-04.05_odp.02}} to disrupt and adversely affect the system or system component.

requirements.discussion: Often, the best method of assessing system resilience is to disrupt the system in some manner. The mechanisms used by the organization could disrupt system functions or system services in many ways, including terminating or disabling critical system components, changing the configuration of system components, degrading critical functionality (e.g., restricting network bandwidth), or altering privileges. Automated, on-going, and simulated cyber-attacks and service disruptions can reveal unexpected functional dependencies and help the organization determine its ability to ensure resilience in the face of an actual cyber-attack.

objectives.text: {{param:cp-04.05_odp.01}} are employed to disrupt and adversely affect the {{param:cp-04.05_odp.02}}.

parameters.label: mechanisms
parameters.guidance: mechanisms employed to disrupt and adversely affect the system or system component are defined;

parameters.label: system or system component
parameters.guidance: system or system component on which to apply disruption mechanisms are defined;

requirements.title: Alternate Storage Site

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Establish an alternate storage site, including necessary agreements to permit the storage and retrieval of system backup information; and

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Ensure that the alternate storage site provides controls equivalent to that of the primary site.

requirements.discussion: Alternate storage sites are geographically distinct from primary storage sites and maintain duplicate copies of information and data if the primary storage site is not available. Similarly, alternate processing sites provide processing capability if the primary processing site is not available. Geographically distributed architectures that support contingency requirements may be considered alternate storage sites. Items covered by alternate storage site agreements include environmental conditions at the alternate sites, access rules for systems and facilities, physical and environmental protection requirements, and coordination of delivery and retrieval of backup media. Alternate storage sites reflect the requirements in contingency plans so that organizations can maintain essential mission and business functions despite compromise, failure, or disruption in organizational systems.

items.label: CP-06a.[01]
items.text: an alternate storage site is established;

items.label: CP-06a.[02]
items.text: establishment of the alternate storage site includes necessary agreements to permit the storage and retrieval of system backup information;

objectives.label: CP-06b.
objectives.text: the alternate storage site provides controls equivalent to that of the primary site.

editorial.question: Does your organization have an alternate storage site for backups, with agreements to store and retrieve them, and protections equal to those at the primary site?
editorial.whyItMatters: Backups kept in the same place as your systems can be lost in the same fire, flood, or attack. A separate storage site with the same protections keeps backups available and secure.
editorial.doneLooksLike: An alternate storage site is established, with agreements that permit storage and retrieval of system backup information, and it provides controls equivalent to those at the primary site. Agreements cover matters such as environmental conditions, access rules, physical protection, and delivery and retrieval of backup media.
nextSteps: Choose an alternate storage location, such as a separate facility or a cloud storage service in another region.
Put agreements in place that cover storage, retrieval, and access.
Confirm the site's security protections match those at your primary site.

requirements.title: Separation from Primary Site

statement.text: Identify an alternate storage site that is sufficiently separated from the primary storage site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats.

requirements.discussion: Threats that affect alternate storage sites are defined in organizational risk assessments and include natural disasters, structural failures, hostile attacks, and errors of omission or commission. Organizations determine what is considered a sufficient degree of separation between primary and alternate storage sites based on the types of threats that are of concern. For threats such as hostile attacks, the degree of separation between sites is less relevant.

objectives.text: an alternate storage site that is sufficiently separated from the primary storage site is identified to reduce susceptibility to the same threats.

editorial.question: Is your alternate storage site far enough from your primary storage site that the same disaster or threat is unlikely to affect both?
editorial.whyItMatters: A backup site in the same building or flood zone could be lost in the same event. Adequate separation keeps at least one copy available.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The alternate storage site you have identified is sufficiently separated from the primary storage site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats, judged against the threats in your risk assessment, such as natural disasters and structural failures.
nextSteps: Review the threats in your risk assessment that could affect both sites, such as regional weather or power outages.
Decide what degree of separation is sufficient for those threats.
Relocate the alternate storage site if it does not meet that separation.

requirements.title: Recovery Time and Recovery Point Objectives

statement.text: Configure the alternate storage site to facilitate recovery operations in accordance with recovery time and recovery point objectives.

requirements.discussion: Organizations establish recovery time and recovery point objectives as part of contingency planning. Configuration of the alternate storage site includes physical facilities and the systems supporting recovery operations that ensure accessibility and correct execution.

objectives.label: CP-06(02)[01]
objectives.text: the alternate storage site is configured to facilitate recovery operations in accordance with recovery time objectives;

objectives.label: CP-06(02)[02]
objectives.text: the alternate storage site is configured to facilitate recovery operations in accordance with recovery point objectives.

editorial.question: Is your alternate storage site set up to meet your recovery time objective (how fast you must recover) and recovery point objective (how much data you can lose)?
editorial.whyItMatters: A backup is useful only if you can restore from it fast enough and it is recent enough. Configuring the storage site around your objectives makes those targets achievable.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The alternate storage site, including its facilities and supporting systems, is configured to facilitate recovery operations in line with your recovery time and recovery point objectives.
nextSteps: Confirm your recovery time and recovery point objectives are documented in the contingency plan.
Check that backup frequency and retrieval speed from the alternate site can meet them.
Adjust storage arrangements where they fall short, and confirm the result through testing.

requirements.title: Accessibility

statement.text: Identify potential accessibility problems to the alternate storage site in the event of an area-wide disruption or disaster and outline explicit mitigation actions.

requirements.discussion: Area-wide disruptions refer to those types of disruptions that are broad in geographic scope with such determinations made by organizations based on organizational assessments of risk. Explicit mitigation actions include duplicating backup information at other alternate storage sites if access problems occur at originally designated alternate sites or planning for physical access to retrieve backup information if electronic accessibility to the alternate site is disrupted.

objectives.label: CP-06(03)[01]
objectives.text: potential accessibility problems to the alternate storage site in the event of an area-wide disruption or disaster are identified;

objectives.label: CP-06(03)[02]
objectives.text: explicit mitigation actions to address identified accessibility problems are outlined.

editorial.question: Has your organization identified what could block access to its alternate storage site during a widespread disaster, and planned how to work around it?
editorial.whyItMatters: A regional disaster can close roads, cut networks, or affect the alternate site itself. Planning ahead means you can still reach your backups.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Potential problems accessing the alternate storage site during an area-wide disruption or disaster are identified, and explicit mitigation actions are outlined, such as duplicating backups at another site or planning physical retrieval if electronic access is lost.
nextSteps: List scenarios that could block access to the alternate storage site, such as network outages or travel restrictions.
Define a mitigation for each, such as a second storage location or physical retrieval.
Record these in the contingency plan.

requirements.title: Alternate Processing Site

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Establish an alternate processing site, including necessary agreements to permit the transfer and resumption of {{param:cp-07_odp.01}} for essential mission and business functions within {{param:cp-07_odp.02}} when the primary processing capabilities are unavailable;

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Make available at the alternate processing site, the equipment and supplies required to transfer and resume operations or put contracts in place to support delivery to the site within the organization-defined time period for transfer and resumption; and

statement.label: c.
statement.text: Provide controls at the alternate processing site that are equivalent to those at the primary site.

requirements.discussion: Alternate processing sites are geographically distinct from primary processing sites and provide processing capability if the primary processing site is not available. The alternate processing capability may be addressed using a physical processing site or other alternatives, such as failover to a cloud-based service provider or other internally or externally provided processing service. Geographically distributed architectures that support contingency requirements may also be considered alternate processing sites. Controls that are covered by alternate processing site agreements include the environmental conditions at alternate sites, access rules, physical and environmental protection requirements, and the coordination for the transfer and assignment of personnel. Requirements are allocated to alternate processing sites that reflect the requirements in contingency plans to maintain essential mission and business functions despite disruption, compromise, or failure in organizational systems.

objectives.label: CP-07a.
objectives.text: an alternate processing site, including necessary agreements to permit the transfer and resumption of {{param:cp-07_odp.01}} for essential mission and business functions, is established within {{param:cp-07_odp.02}} when the primary processing capabilities are unavailable;

items.label: CP-07b.[01]
items.text: the equipment and supplies required to transfer operations are made available at the alternate processing site or if contracts are in place to support delivery to the site within {{param:cp-07_odp.02}} for transfer;

items.label: CP-07b.[02]
items.text: the equipment and supplies required to resume operations are made available at the alternate processing site or if contracts are in place to support delivery to the site within {{param:cp-07_odp.02}} for resumption;

objectives.label: CP-07c.
objectives.text: controls provided at the alternate processing site are equivalent to those at the primary site.

parameters.label: system operations
parameters.guidance: system operations for essential mission and business functions are defined;

parameters.label: time period
parameters.guidance: time period consistent with recovery time and recovery point objectives is defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization have an alternate processing site, with agreements, equipment, and protections in place, to resume essential operations within a defined time if the primary site fails?
editorial.whyItMatters: If your main site or service fails, you need somewhere else to run essential systems. Arrangements made ahead of time work far faster than ones made during a crisis.
editorial.doneLooksLike: An alternate processing site, such as a second facility or a cloud service, is established with agreements that permit transfer and resumption of the system operations you define for essential functions within the time period you define. The equipment and supplies needed to transfer and resume operations are at the site, or contracts are in place for delivery within that time, and the site provides controls equivalent to those at the primary site.
nextSteps: Decide which operations must move and how quickly.
Select an alternate processing option, and put agreements in place.
Arrange equipment and supplies at the site, or contracts for timely delivery.
Confirm the alternate site's security protections match those at your primary site.

requirements.title: Separation from Primary Site

statement.text: Identify an alternate processing site that is sufficiently separated from the primary processing site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats.

requirements.discussion: Threats that affect alternate processing sites are defined in organizational assessments of risk and include natural disasters, structural failures, hostile attacks, and errors of omission or commission. Organizations determine what is considered a sufficient degree of separation between primary and alternate processing sites based on the types of threats that are of concern. For threats such as hostile attacks, the degree of separation between sites is less relevant.

objectives.text: an alternate processing site that is sufficiently separated from the primary processing site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats is identified.

editorial.question: Is your alternate processing site far enough from your primary processing site that the same disaster or threat is unlikely to disable both?
editorial.whyItMatters: If both sites share the same power grid, flood zone, or building, one event could take out both. Separation keeps processing available.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The alternate processing site you have identified is sufficiently separated from the primary processing site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats, judged against the threats identified in your risk assessment.
nextSteps: Identify threats that could affect both sites, such as regional disasters or shared infrastructure.
Decide what degree of separation is sufficient.
If you use a cloud provider, choose a region distinct from your primary processing location.

requirements.title: Accessibility

statement.text: Identify potential accessibility problems to alternate processing sites in the event of an area-wide disruption or disaster and outlines explicit mitigation actions.

requirements.discussion: Area-wide disruptions refer to those types of disruptions that are broad in geographic scope with such determinations made by organizations based on organizational assessments of risk.

objectives.label: CP-07(02)[01]
objectives.text: potential accessibility problems to alternate processing sites in the event of an area-wide disruption or disaster are identified;

objectives.label: CP-07(02)[02]
objectives.text: explicit mitigation actions to address identified accessibility problems are outlined.

editorial.question: Has your organization identified what could prevent it from using its alternate processing site during a widespread disaster, and planned how to address it?
editorial.whyItMatters: In a regional event, staff may be unable to travel or networks may be down, making an alternate site unusable when it is needed. Planning ahead keeps the site reachable.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Potential problems accessing alternate processing sites during an area-wide disruption or disaster are identified, and explicit mitigation actions are outlined.
nextSteps: List what could block staff or network access to the alternate processing site.
Define mitigations, such as remote access arrangements or a secondary site.
Document them in the contingency plan, and test them where practical.

requirements.title: Priority of Service

statement.text: Develop alternate processing site agreements that contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements (including recovery time objectives).

requirements.discussion: Priority of service agreements refer to negotiated agreements with service providers that ensure that organizations receive priority treatment consistent with their availability requirements and the availability of information resources for logical alternate processing and/or at the physical alternate processing site. Organizations establish recovery time objectives as part of contingency planning.

objectives.text: alternate processing site agreements that contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements (including recovery time objectives) are developed.

editorial.question: Do your alternate processing site agreements include priority-of-service terms that reflect your availability needs, including your recovery time objectives?
editorial.whyItMatters: In a regional disaster, many customers may compete for the same provider's resources. Priority terms help you get service quickly enough to meet your recovery goals.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Alternate processing site agreements contain priority-of-service provisions consistent with your availability requirements, including recovery time objectives.
nextSteps: Review current agreements with alternate processing providers.
Negotiate priority-of-service terms aligned with your recovery time objectives.
Record the agreed terms in the contingency plan.

requirements.title: Preparation for Use

statement.text: Prepare the alternate processing site so that the site can serve as the operational site supporting essential mission and business functions.

requirements.discussion: Site preparation includes establishing configuration settings for systems at the alternate processing site consistent with the requirements for such settings at the primary site and ensuring that essential supplies and logistical considerations are in place.

objectives.text: the alternate processing site is prepared so that the site can serve as the operational site supporting essential mission and business functions.

editorial.question: Is your alternate processing site prepared, with matching configuration settings, supplies, and logistics, to serve as your operational site for essential functions?
editorial.whyItMatters: An alternate site that still needs setting up when disaster strikes will delay recovery. Preparing it ahead means you can switch over when needed.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The alternate processing site is prepared to serve as the operational site supporting essential mission and business functions, with system configuration settings consistent with those at the primary site and essential supplies and logistics in place.
nextSteps: Apply your primary site's configuration settings to systems at the alternate site, and keep them in sync.
Stock essential supplies, and plan logistics such as staff access and transport.
Verify readiness periodically through testing.

requirements.title: Inability to Return to Primary Site

statement.text: Plan and prepare for circumstances that preclude returning to the primary processing site.

requirements.discussion: There may be situations that preclude an organization from returning to the primary processing site such as if a natural disaster (e.g., flood or a hurricane) damaged or destroyed a facility and it was determined that rebuilding in the same location was not prudent.

objectives.label: CP-07(06)[01]
objectives.text: circumstances that preclude returning to the primary processing site are planned for;

objectives.label: CP-07(06)[02]
objectives.text: circumstances that preclude returning to the primary processing site are prepared for.

requirements.title: Telecommunications Services

statement.text: Establish alternate telecommunications services, including necessary agreements to permit the resumption of {{param:cp-08_odp.01}} for essential mission and business functions within {{param:cp-08_odp.02}} when the primary telecommunications capabilities are unavailable at either the primary or alternate processing or storage sites.

requirements.discussion: Telecommunications services (for data and voice) for primary and alternate processing and storage sites are in scope for CP-8 . Alternate telecommunications services reflect the continuity requirements in contingency plans to maintain essential mission and business functions despite the loss of primary telecommunications services. Organizations may specify different time periods for primary or alternate sites. Alternate telecommunications services include additional organizational or commercial ground-based circuits or lines, network-based approaches to telecommunications, or the use of satellites. Organizations consider factors such as availability, quality of service, and access when entering into alternate telecommunications agreements.

objectives.text: alternate telecommunications services, including necessary agreements to permit the resumption of {{param:cp-08_odp.01}} , are established for essential mission and business functions within {{param:cp-08_odp.02}} when the primary telecommunications capabilities are unavailable at either the primary or alternate processing or storage sites.

parameters.label: system operations
parameters.guidance: system operations to be resumed for essential mission and business functions are defined;

parameters.label: time period
parameters.guidance: time period within which to resume essential mission and business functions when the primary telecommunications capabilities are unavailable is defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization have alternate telecommunications services, with agreements in place, to resume essential operations within a defined time if primary data or voice services fail?
editorial.whyItMatters: Losing internet or phone service can stop operations even when systems are running. Alternate services keep essential functions connected.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Alternate telecommunications services for data and voice, with the necessary agreements, are established to permit resumption of the system operations you define for essential functions within the time period you define when primary telecommunications are unavailable at the primary or alternate processing or storage sites.
nextSteps: Identify the communications services your essential functions depend on at each site.
Arrange alternate services, such as a second internet provider, cellular backup, or satellite.
Put agreements in place, and confirm they support your resumption time.

requirements.title: Priority of Service Provisions

statement.label: (a)
statement.text: Develop primary and alternate telecommunications service agreements that contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements (including recovery time objectives); and

statement.label: (b)
statement.text: Request Telecommunications Service Priority for all telecommunications services used for national security emergency preparedness if the primary and/or alternate telecommunications services are provided by a common carrier.

requirements.discussion: Organizations consider the potential mission or business impact in situations where telecommunications service providers are servicing other organizations with similar priority of service provisions. Telecommunications Service Priority (TSP) is a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) program that directs telecommunications service providers (e.g., wireline and wireless phone companies) to give preferential treatment to users enrolled in the program when they need to add new lines or have their lines restored following a disruption of service, regardless of the cause. The FCC sets the rules and policies for the TSP program, and the Department of Homeland Security manages the TSP program. The TSP program is always in effect and not contingent on a major disaster or attack taking place. Federal sponsorship is required to enroll in the TSP program.

items.label: CP-08(01)(a)[01]
items.text: primary telecommunications service agreements that contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements (including recovery time objectives) are developed;

items.label: CP-08(01)(a)[02]
items.text: alternate telecommunications service agreements that contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements (including recovery time objectives) are developed;

objectives.label: CP-08(01)(b)
objectives.text: Telecommunications Service Priority is requested for all telecommunications services used for national security emergency preparedness if the primary and/or alternate telecommunications services are provided by a common carrier.

editorial.question: Do your primary and alternate telecommunications agreements include priority-of-service terms that match your availability needs and recovery time objectives?
editorial.whyItMatters: During widespread outages, providers restore service in priority order. Priority terms help you get reconnected in time to meet your recovery objectives.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Primary and alternate telecommunications service agreements contain priority-of-service provisions consistent with your availability requirements, including recovery time objectives. If services used for national security emergency preparedness come from a common carrier, you have requested Telecommunications Service Priority, a federally sponsored program that gives enrolled users preference when lines are added or restored.
nextSteps: Review your telecommunications agreements for priority-of-service terms, and negotiate them where missing.
Align those terms with your recovery time objectives.
Determine whether any services support national security emergency preparedness, and if so, request Telecommunications Service Priority through a federal sponsor.

requirements.title: Single Points of Failure

statement.text: Obtain alternate telecommunications services to reduce the likelihood of sharing a single point of failure with primary telecommunications services.

requirements.discussion: In certain circumstances, telecommunications service providers or services may share the same physical lines, which increases the vulnerability of a single failure point. It is important to have provider transparency for the actual physical transmission capability for telecommunication services.

objectives.text: alternate telecommunications services to reduce the likelihood of sharing a single point of failure with primary telecommunications services are obtained.

editorial.question: Are your alternate telecommunications services arranged so they do not share a single point of failure, such as the same physical line, with your primary services?
editorial.whyItMatters: Two services that run over the same cable or building entry point can fail together. Avoiding shared points of failure keeps the backup working when the primary goes down.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Alternate telecommunications services are obtained that reduce the likelihood of sharing a single point of failure with primary services, informed by information from providers about the physical paths their services use.
nextSteps: Ask providers how their services physically reach your sites.
Identify shared lines, conduits, or equipment between primary and alternate services.
Choose alternate services that use different paths, such as a wireless or satellite link.

requirements.title: Separation of Primary and Alternate Providers

statement.text: Obtain alternate telecommunications services from providers that are separated from primary service providers to reduce susceptibility to the same threats.

requirements.discussion: Threats that affect telecommunications services are defined in organizational assessments of risk and include natural disasters, structural failures, cyber or physical attacks, and errors of omission or commission. Organizations can reduce common susceptibilities by minimizing shared infrastructure among telecommunications service providers and achieving sufficient geographic separation between services. Organizations may consider using a single service provider in situations where the service provider can provide alternate telecommunications services that meet the separation needs addressed in the risk assessment.

objectives.text: alternate telecommunications services from providers that are separated from primary service providers are obtained to reduce susceptibility to the same threats.

editorial.question: Does your organization get alternate telecommunications services from providers separated enough from the primary provider that the same threat is unlikely to affect both?
editorial.whyItMatters: Providers that share infrastructure or a region can be affected by the same disaster, attack, or error. Separation reduces the chance of losing both at once.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Alternate telecommunications services are obtained from providers separated from primary providers to reduce susceptibility to the same threats, for example by minimizing shared infrastructure and achieving geographic separation. A single provider may be used if it can deliver alternate services that meet the separation needs in your risk assessment.
nextSteps: Review your risk assessment for threats that could affect telecommunications.
Compare primary and alternate providers for shared infrastructure and geography.
Change alternate providers or service arrangements where separation is insufficient.

requirements.title: Provider Contingency Plan

statement.label: (a)
statement.text: Require primary and alternate telecommunications service providers to have contingency plans;

statement.label: (b)
statement.text: Review provider contingency plans to ensure that the plans meet organizational contingency requirements; and

statement.label: (c)
statement.text: Obtain evidence of contingency testing and training by providers {{param:cp-8.4_prm_1}}.

requirements.discussion: Reviews of provider contingency plans consider the proprietary nature of such plans. In some situations, a summary of provider contingency plans may be sufficient evidence for organizations to satisfy the review requirement. Telecommunications service providers may also participate in ongoing disaster recovery exercises in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security and state and local governments. Organizations may use these types of activities to satisfy evidentiary requirements related to service provider contingency plan reviews, testing, and training.

editorial.question: Does your organization require its telecommunications providers to have contingency plans, review those plans, and obtain evidence that providers test and train on them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Your continuity depends partly on your providers' ability to recover. Reviewing their plans and evidence of testing shows whether they can support you through a disruption.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Primary and alternate telecommunications providers are required to have contingency plans, those plans are reviewed to confirm they meet your contingency requirements, and evidence of provider contingency testing and training is obtained at the frequencies you define. Where a provider's full plan is proprietary, a summary may be sufficient.
nextSteps: Add a contingency plan requirement to provider agreements.

statement.text: Test alternate telecommunication services {{param:cp-08.05_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Alternate telecommunications services testing is arranged through contractual agreements with service providers. The testing may occur in parallel with normal operations to ensure that there is no degradation in organizational missions or functions.

requirements.title: System Backup

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Conduct backups of user-level information contained in {{param:cp-09_odp.01}} {{param:cp-09_odp.02}};

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Conduct backups of system-level information contained in the system {{param:cp-09_odp.03}};

statement.label: c.
statement.text: Conduct backups of system documentation, including security- and privacy-related documentation {{param:cp-09_odp.04}} ; and

statement.label: d.
statement.text: Protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of backup information.

requirements.discussion: System-level information includes system state information, operating system software, middleware, application software, and licenses. User-level information includes information other than system-level information. Mechanisms employed to protect the integrity of system backups include digital signatures and cryptographic hashes. Protection of system backup information while in transit is addressed by MP-5 and SC-8 . System backups reflect the requirements in contingency plans as well as other organizational requirements for backing up information. Organizations may be subject to laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, or policies with requirements regarding specific categories of information (e.g., personal health information). Organizational personnel consult with the senior agency official for privacy and legal counsel regarding such requirements.

editorial.question: Does your organization back up user data, system-level information, and system documentation on schedules it defines, and protect those backups?
editorial.whyItMatters: Backups are often the only way to recover from ransomware, hardware failure, or accidental deletion. Backups that are missing, out of date, or exposed can turn a recoverable event into a lasting loss.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Backups of user-level information on the components you define, of system-level information such as operating systems, applications, and configurations, and of system documentation, including security and privacy documentation, are taken at the frequencies you define. The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of backup information are protected, for example through encryption, access restrictions, and integrity checks.

requirements.title: Testing for Reliability and Integrity

statement.text: Test backup information {{param:cp-9.1_prm_1}} to verify media reliability and information integrity.

requirements.discussion: Organizations need assurance that backup information can be reliably retrieved. Reliability pertains to the systems and system components where the backup information is stored, the operations used to retrieve the information, and the integrity of the information being retrieved. Independent and specialized tests can be used for each of the aspects of reliability. For example, decrypting and transporting (or transmitting) a random sample of backup files from the alternate storage or backup site and comparing the information to the same information at the primary processing site can provide such assurance.

editorial.question: Does your organization test its backups at a frequency it defines to confirm the storage media are reliable and the information is intact?
editorial.whyItMatters: Backups can fail silently through damaged media, incomplete jobs, or corruption. Testing reveals problems before you need to restore in an emergency.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Backup information is tested at the frequency you define to verify media reliability and information integrity, for example by retrieving a sample of backup files and comparing them with the originals.
nextSteps: Set a backup testing frequency.

requirements.title: Test Restoration Using Sampling

statement.text: Use a sample of backup information in the restoration of selected system functions as part of contingency plan testing.

requirements.discussion: Organizations need assurance that system functions can be restored correctly and can support established organizational missions. To ensure that the selected system functions are thoroughly exercised during contingency plan testing, a sample of backup information is retrieved to determine whether the functions are operating as intended. Organizations can determine the sample size for the functions and backup information based on the level of assurance needed.

objectives.text: a sample of backup information in the restoration of selected system functions is used as part of contingency plan testing.

editorial.question: As part of contingency plan testing, does your organization restore selected system functions from a sample of backup information to confirm they work?
editorial.whyItMatters: Being able to read a backup file is not the same as getting a working system back. Restoring real functions from backups during tests shows that recovery will work.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Contingency plan testing includes using a sample of backup information to restore selected system functions and confirming that those functions operate as intended. You choose the sample size based on the level of assurance you need.
nextSteps: Select system functions to restore during your next contingency test.
Restore them from backup data, and confirm they operate correctly.
Record the results, and fix gaps in backup or restoration procedures.

requirements.title: Separate Storage for Critical Information

statement.text: Store backup copies of {{param:cp-09.03_odp}} in a separate facility or in a fire rated container that is not collocated with the operational system.

requirements.discussion: Separate storage for critical information applies to all critical information regardless of the type of backup storage media. Critical system software includes operating systems, middleware, cryptographic key management systems, and intrusion detection systems. Security-related information includes inventories of system hardware, software, and firmware components. Alternate storage sites, including geographically distributed architectures, serve as separate storage facilities for organizations. Organizations may provide separate storage by implementing automated backup processes at alternative storage sites (e.g., data centers). The General Services Administration (GSA) establishes standards and specifications for security and fire rated containers.

editorial.doneLooksLike: Backup copies of the critical system software and other security-related information you define, such as operating systems, key management systems, and component inventories, are stored in a separate facility or in a fire-rated container that is not collocated with the operational system.

If this type of redundancy is in place and there is sufficient geographic separation between the two systems, the secondary system can also serve as the alternate processing site.

requirements.discussion: Dual authorization ensures that deletion or destruction of backup information cannot occur unless two qualified individuals carry out the task. Individuals deleting or destroying backup information possess the skills or expertise to determine if the proposed deletion or destruction of information reflects organizational policies and procedures. Dual authorization may also be known as two-person control. To reduce the risk of collusion, organizations consider rotating dual authorization duties to other individuals.

requirements.title: System Recovery and Reconstitution

statement.text: Provide for the recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state within {{param:cp-10_prm_1}} after a disruption, compromise, or failure.

requirements.discussion: Recovery is executing contingency plan activities to restore organizational mission and business functions. Reconstitution takes place following recovery and includes activities for returning systems to fully operational states. Recovery and reconstitution operations reflect mission and business priorities; recovery point, recovery time, and reconstitution objectives; and organizational metrics consistent with contingency plan requirements. Reconstitution includes the deactivation of interim system capabilities that may have been needed during recovery operations. Reconstitution also includes assessments of fully restored system capabilities, reestablishment of continuous monitoring activities, system reauthorization (if required), and activities to prepare the system and organization for future disruptions, breaches, compromises, or failures. Recovery and reconstitution capabilities can include automated mechanisms and manual procedures. Organizations establish recovery time and recovery point objectives as part of contingency planning.

editorial.doneLooksLike: After a disruption, compromise, or failure, you can recover the system and reconstitute it to a known state within the time period you define, consistent with your recovery time objective (how long you can be without the system) and recovery point objective (how much recent data you can afford to lose). Reconstitution includes returning the system to full operation and deactivating any temporary capabilities used during recovery.

editorial.question: For transaction-based systems, such as databases, does your organization have transaction recovery in place so data returns to a consistent state after a failure?
editorial.whyItMatters: A failure in the middle of transactions can leave data inconsistent, such as an order recorded without its payment. Transaction recovery undoes or completes partial work so records stay reliable.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Transaction recovery is implemented for transaction-based systems, such as database management and transaction processing systems, using mechanisms such as transaction rollback and transaction journaling (a running log of changes that can be replayed or undone).

statement.text: Employ {{param:cp-13_odp.01}} for satisfying {{param:cp-13_odp.02}} when the primary means of implementing the security function is unavailable or compromised.

requirements.discussion: Use of alternative security mechanisms supports system resiliency, contingency planning, and continuity of operations. To ensure mission and business continuity, organizations can implement alternative or supplemental security mechanisms. The mechanisms may be less effective than the primary mechanisms. However, having the capability to readily employ alternative or supplemental mechanisms enhances mission and business continuity that might otherwise be adversely impacted if operations had to be curtailed until the primary means of implementing the functions was restored. Given the cost and level of effort required to provide such alternative capabilities, the alternative or supplemental mechanisms are only applied to critical security capabilities provided by systems, system components, or system services. requirements.discussion: Identification and authentication policy and procedures address the controls in the IA family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance. Therefore, it is important that security and privacy programs collaborate on the development of identification and authentication policy and procedures. Security and privacy program policies and procedures at the organization level are preferable, in general, and may obviate the need for mission- or system-specific policies and procedures. The policy can be included as part of the general security and privacy policy or be represented by multiple policies that reflect the complex nature of organizations. Procedures can be established for security and privacy programs, for mission or business processes, and for systems, if needed. Procedures describe how the policies or controls are implemented and can be directed at the individual or role that is the object of the procedure. Procedures can be documented in system security and privacy plans or in one or more separate documents. Events that may precipitate an update to identification and authentication policy and procedures include assessment or audit findings, security incidents or breaches, or changes in applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Simply restating controls does not constitute an organizational policy or procedure.

editorial.question: Does your organization have a documented identification and authentication policy and procedures, covering how users and devices prove who they are, with a named owner and regular reviews?
editorial.whyItMatters: How people log on determines how hard it is for an attacker to pose as them. A policy and procedures set consistent rules for identifiers, passwords, multi-factor authentication, and other credentials across your systems.
editorial.doneLooksLike: A documented identification and authentication policy, at the organization, business process, or system level you choose, addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among teams, and compliance, and is consistent with applicable laws and regulations. Procedures describe how identifiers are assigned and how authenticators such as passwords, tokens, and certificates are issued, managed, and revoked. Both are distributed to the people or roles you define, managed by a designated official, and reviewed and updated at the frequency and after the events you define.

requirements.title: Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)

statement.text: Uniquely identify and authenticate organizational users and associate that unique identification with processes acting on behalf of those users.

requirements.discussion:
Organizations can satisfy the identification and authentication requirements by complying with the requirements in HSPD 12 . Organizational users include employees or individuals who organizations consider to have an equivalent status to employees (e.g., contractors and guest researchers). Unique identification and authentication of users applies to all accesses other than those that are explicitly identified in AC-14 and that occur through the authorized use of group authenticators without individual authentication. Since processes execute on behalf of groups and roles, organizations may require unique identification of individuals in group accounts or for detailed accountability of individual activity.

Organizations employ passwords, physical authenticators, or biometrics to authenticate user identities or, in the case of multi-factor authentication, some combination thereof. Access to organizational systems is defined as either local access or network access. Local access is any access to organizational systems by users or processes acting on behalf of users, where access is obtained through direct connections without the use of networks. Network access is access to organizational systems by users (or processes acting on behalf of users) where access is obtained through network connections (i.e., nonlocal accesses). Remote access is a type of network access that involves communication through external networks. Internal networks include local area networks and wide area networks.

The use of encrypted virtual private networks for network connections between organization-controlled endpoints and non-organization-controlled endpoints may be treated as internal networks with respect to protecting the confidentiality and integrity of information traversing the network. Identification and authentication requirements for non-organizational users are described in IA-8.

objectives.label: IA-02[01]
objectives.text: organizational users are uniquely identified and authenticated;

objectives.label: IA-02[02]
objectives.text: the unique identification of authenticated organizational users is associated with processes acting on behalf of those users.

editorial.question: Does every person in your organization log on with their own unique account, so actions on your systems can be traced back to the individual?
editorial.whyItMatters: Shared logons make it impossible to know who did what, and a single leaked shared password exposes everyone who uses it. Unique identification is the basis for accountability and for most other access controls.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Organizational users, including employees and others treated like employees such as contractors, are uniquely identified and authenticated, and processes running on their behalf are associated with their identity. Exceptions are limited to actions documented as permitted without identification (AC-14) and authorized use of group authenticators.
nextSteps: Replace shared logons with individual accounts wherever possible.
Confirm every user authenticates with credentials only they hold.
Document any remaining shared or anonymous access and the reason it is permitted.

requirements.title: Multi-factor Authentication to Privileged Accounts

statement.text: Implement multi-factor authentication for access to privileged accounts.

requirements.discussion: Multi-factor authentication requires the use of two or more different factors to achieve authentication. The authentication factors are defined as follows: something you know (e.g., a personal identification number [PIN]), something you have (e.g., a physical authenticator such as a cryptographic private key), or something you are (e.g., a biometric). Multi-factor authentication solutions that feature physical authenticators include hardware authenticators that provide time-based or challenge-response outputs and smart cards such as the U.S. Government Personal Identity Verification (PIV) card or the Department of Defense (DoD) Common Access Card (CAC). In addition to authenticating users at the system level (i.e., at logon), organizations may employ authentication mechanisms at the application level, at their discretion, to provide increased security. Regardless of the type of access (i.e., local, network, remote), privileged accounts are authenticated using multi-factor options appropriate for the level of risk. Organizations can add additional security measures, such as additional or more rigorous authentication mechanisms, for specific types of access.

objectives.text: multi-factor authentication is implemented for access to privileged accounts.

editorial.question: Do administrator and other privileged accounts require multi-factor authentication, a second check beyond a password, whether access is local, over the network, or remote?
editorial.whyItMatters: Privileged accounts can change settings, read all data, and turn off protections, so they are prime targets. Requiring a second factor means a stolen password alone is not enough to take control.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Multi-factor authentication, using two or more different factors such as something you know, something you have, or something you are, is implemented for all access to privileged accounts, whether local, network, or remote.
nextSteps: Identify all privileged accounts, including cloud administrator, server administrator, and network device accounts.
Turn on multi-factor authentication for each, using an authenticator app, hardware key, or smart card.
Confirm no privileged account can sign in with a password alone.

requirements.title: Multi-factor Authentication to Non-privileged Accounts

statement.text: Implement multi-factor authentication for access to non-privileged accounts.

requirements.discussion: Multi-factor authentication requires the use of two or more different factors to achieve authentication. The authentication factors are defined as follows: something you know (e.g., a personal identification number [PIN]), something you have (e.g., a physical authenticator such as a cryptographic private key), or something you are (e.g., a biometric). Multi-factor authentication solutions that feature physical authenticators include hardware authenticators that provide time-based or challenge-response outputs and smart cards such as the U.S. Government Personal Identity Verification card or the DoD Common Access Card. In addition to authenticating users at the system level, organizations may also employ authentication mechanisms at the application level, at their discretion, to provide increased information security. Regardless of the type of access (i.e., local, network, remote), non-privileged accounts are authenticated using multi-factor options appropriate for the level of risk. Organizations can provide additional security measures, such as additional or more rigorous authentication mechanisms, for specific types of access.

objectives.text: multi-factor authentication for access to non-privileged accounts is implemented.

editorial.question: Do regular, non-administrator user accounts also require multi-factor authentication, a second check beyond a password, when people sign in?
editorial.whyItMatters: Phishing and password reuse put ordinary accounts at constant risk, and a compromised user account is often an attacker's first foothold. Multi-factor authentication makes a stolen password far less useful.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Multi-factor authentication is implemented for access to non-privileged accounts, whether local, network, or remote, using options appropriate to the level of risk.
nextSteps: Enable multi-factor authentication for all user accounts in your email, cloud, and remote access services.
Help staff enroll an authenticator app or security key.
Extend multi-factor authentication to local and network logons on the system.

requirements.title: Individual Authentication with Group Authentication

statement.text: When shared accounts or authenticators are employed, require users to be individually authenticated before granting access to the shared accounts or resources.

requirements.discussion: Individual authentication prior to shared group authentication mitigates the risk of using group accounts or authenticators.

objectives.text: users are required to be individually authenticated before granting access to the shared accounts or resources when shared accounts or authenticators are employed.

editorial.question: When shared accounts or shared credentials are used, does your organization require each person to sign in individually before gaining access to them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Shared accounts make it hard to know who did what. Requiring individual sign-in first ties each use of a shared account to a specific person.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Where shared accounts or authenticators are used, each user is individually authenticated before being granted access to the shared accounts or resources.
nextSteps: Identify the shared accounts and shared credentials in use.
Require individual sign-in before access, for example through a privileged access tool or by having users sign in as themselves before switching to the shared account.
Remove shared accounts that are no longer needed.

requirements.title: Access to Accounts —separate Device

statement.text: Implement multi-factor authentication for {{param:ia-02.06_odp.01}} access to {{param:ia-02.06_odp.02}} such that:

items.label: (a)
items.text: One of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system gaining access; and

items.label: (b)
items.text: The device meets {{param:ia-02.06_odp.03}}.

requirements.discussion: The purpose of requiring a device that is separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access for one of the factors during multi-factor authentication is to reduce the likelihood of compromising authenticators or credentials stored on the system. Adversaries may be able to compromise such authenticators or credentials and subsequently impersonate authorized users. Implementing one of the factors on a separate device (e.g., a hardware token), provides a greater strength of mechanism and an increased level of assurance in the authentication process.

objectives.label: IA-02(06)(a)
objectives.text: multi-factor authentication is implemented for {{param:ia-02.06_odp.01}} access to {{param:ia-02.06_odp.02}} such that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system gaining access;

objectives.label: IA-02(06)(b)
objectives.text: multi-factor authentication is implemented for {{param:ia-02.06_odp.01}} access to {{param:ia-02.06_odp.02}} such that the device meets {{param:ia-02.06_odp.03}}.

requirements.title: Access to Accounts — Replay Resistant

statement.text: Implement replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for access to {{param:ia-02.08_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Authentication processes resist replay attacks if it is impractical to achieve successful authentications by replaying previous authentication messages. Replay-resistant techniques include protocols that use nonces or challenges such as time synchronous or cryptographic authenticators.

objectives.text: replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for access to {{param:ia-02.08_odp}} are implemented.

editorial.question: Does your organization use authentication methods that resist replay, so a captured logon cannot be reused, for the privileged or non-privileged accounts it has selected?
editorial.whyItMatters: If an attacker can capture authentication traffic and send it again, they may be able to log in without knowing the password. Replay-resistant methods make each logon unique, so recorded logons cannot be reused.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Replay-resistant authentication mechanisms, such as protocols that use one-time challenges, time-based codes, or cryptographic authenticators, are implemented for access to the account types you have selected: privileged accounts, non-privileged accounts, or both.
nextSteps: Decide which account types this applies to.
Confirm your authentication methods use challenges, time-based one-time codes, or cryptographic authenticators.
Retire older logon protocols that send reusable credentials.

requirements.title: Single Sign-on

statement.text: Provide a single sign-on capability for {{param:ia-02.10_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Single sign-on enables users to log in once and gain access to multiple system resources. Organizations consider the operational efficiencies provided by single sign-on capabilities with the risk introduced by allowing access to multiple systems via a single authentication event. Single sign-on can present opportunities to improve system security, for example by providing the ability to add multi-factor authentication for applications and systems (existing and new) that may not be able to natively support multi-factor authentication.

objectives.text: a single sign-on capability is provided for {{param:ia-02.10_odp}}.

parameters.label: system accounts and services
parameters.guidance: system accounts and services for which a single sign-on capability must be provided are defined;

requirements.title: Acceptance of PIV Credentials

statement.text: Accept and electronically verify Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials.

requirements.discussion: Acceptance of Personal Identity Verification (PIV)-compliant credentials applies to organizations implementing logical access control and physical access control systems. PIV-compliant credentials are those credentials issued by federal agencies that conform to FIPS Publication 201 and supporting guidance documents. The adequacy and reliability of PIV card issuers are authorized using SP 800-79-2 . Acceptance of PIV-compliant credentials includes derived PIV credentials, the use of which is addressed in SP 800-166 . The DOD Common Access Card (CAC) is an example of a PIV credential.

objectives.text: Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials are accepted and electronically verified.

editorial.question: Do your systems accept and electronically verify Personal Identity Verification (PIV) credentials, the federal government's standard smart card identity credential?
editorial.whyItMatters: PIV credentials provide strong, government-issued proof of identity. Accepting and electronically verifying them lets federal users authenticate with a trusted credential rather than a password alone.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Your logical and physical access control systems accept credentials that conform to the PIV standard, including derived PIV credentials where used, and verify them electronically.
nextSteps: Determine whether your users hold PIV or derived PIV credentials.
Configure systems and applications to accept these credentials for logon and, where relevant, physical entry.
Confirm credentials are electronically verified, including checks that they are valid and not revoked.

requirements.title: Out-of-band Authentication

statement.text: Implement the following out-of-band authentication mechanisms under {{param:ia-02.13_odp.02}}: {{param:ia-02.13_odp.01}}.

requirements.discussion: Out-of-band authentication refers to the use of two separate communication paths to identify and authenticate users or devices to an information system. The first path (i.e., the in-band path) is used to identify and authenticate users or devices and is generally the path through which information flows. The second path (i.e., the out-of-band path) is used to independently verify the authentication and/or requested action. For example, a user authenticates via a notebook computer to a remote server to which the user desires access and requests some action of the server via that communication path. Subsequently, the server contacts the user via the user’s cell phone to verify that the requested action originated from the user. The user may confirm the intended action to an individual on the telephone or provide an authentication code via the telephone. Out-of-band authentication can be used to mitigate actual or suspected "man-in the-middle" attacks. The conditions or criteria for activation include suspicious activities, new threat indicators, elevated threat levels, or the impact or classification level of information in requested transactions.

objectives.text: {{param:ia-02.13_odp.01}} mechanisms are implemented under {{param:ia-02.13_odp.02}}.

requirements.title: Device Identification and Authentication

statement.text: Uniquely identify and authenticate {{param:ia-03_odp.01}} before establishing a {{param:ia-03_odp.02}} connection.

requirements.discussion: Devices that require unique device-to-device identification and authentication are defined by type, device, or a combination of type and device. Organization-defined device types include devices that are not owned by the organization. Systems use shared known information (e.g., Media Access Control [MAC], Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol [TCP/IP] addresses) for device identification or organizational authentication solutions (e.g., Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1x and Extensible Authentication Protocol [EAP], RADIUS server with EAP-Transport Layer Security [TLS] authentication, Kerberos) to identify and authenticate devices on local and wide area networks. Organizations determine the required strength of authentication mechanisms based on the security categories of systems and mission or business requirements. Because of the challenges of implementing device authentication on a large scale, organizations can restrict the application of the control to a limited number/type of devices based on mission or business needs.

objectives.text: {{param:ia-03_odp.01}} are uniquely identified and authenticated before establishing a {{param:ia-03_odp.02}} connection.

parameters.label: devices and/or types of devices
parameters.guidance: devices and/or types of devices to be uniquely identified and authenticated before establishing a connection are defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization uniquely identify and authenticate the devices it specifies before letting them make local, remote, or network connections?
editorial.whyItMatters: Unknown devices on your network can be used to steal data or launch attacks. Requiring devices to prove their identity keeps unauthorized equipment from connecting.
editorial.doneLooksLike: The devices or types of devices you define, which may include devices your organization does not own, are uniquely identified and authenticated before establishing the types of connection you have selected: local, remote, network, or a combination. Authentication strength reflects the system's security category and business needs.
nextSteps: Decide which devices or types of devices must authenticate, and for which kinds of connection.
Use network access control or certificate-based device authentication to enforce it.
Maintain a record of authorized devices, and review connection attempts from unknown ones.

requirements.title: Cryptographic Bidirectional Authentication

statement.text: Authenticate {{param:ia-03.01_odp.01}} before establishing {{param:ia-03.01_odp.02}} connection using bidirectional authentication that is cryptographically based.

requirements.discussion: A local connection is a connection with a device that communicates without the use of a network. A network connection is a connection with a device that communicates through a network. A remote connection is a connection with a device that communicates through an external network. Bidirectional authentication provides stronger protection to validate the identity of other devices for connections that are of greater risk.

objectives.text: {{param:ia-03.01_odp.01}} are authenticated before establishing {{param:ia-03.01_odp.02}} connection using bidirectional authentication that is cryptographically based.

parameters.label: devices and/or types of devices

requirements.title: Device Attestation

statement.text: Handle device identification and authentication based on attestation by {{param:ia-03.04_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Device attestation refers to the identification and authentication of a device based on its configuration and known operating state. Device attestation can be determined via a cryptographic hash of the device. If device attestation is the means of identification and authentication, then it is important that patches and updates to the device are handled via a configuration management process such that the patches and updates are done securely and do not disrupt identification and authentication to other devices.

requirements.title: Identifier Management

statement.text: Manage system identifiers by:

items.label: a.
items.text: Receiving authorization from {{param:ia-04_odp.01}} to assign an individual, group, role, service, or device identifier;

items.label: b.
items.text: Selecting an identifier that identifies an individual, group, role, service, or device;

items.label: c.
items.text: Assigning the identifier to the intended individual, group, role, service, or device; and

items.label: d.
items.text: Preventing reuse of identifiers for {{param:ia-04_odp.02}}.

requirements.discussion: Common device identifiers include Media Access Control (MAC) addresses, Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, or device-unique token identifiers. The management of individual identifiers is not applicable to shared system accounts. Typically, individual identifiers are the usernames of the system accounts assigned to those individuals. In such instances, the account management activities of AC-2 use account names provided by IA-4 . Identifier management also addresses individual identifiers not necessarily associated with system accounts. Preventing the reuse of identifiers implies preventing the assignment of previously used individual, group, role, service, or device identifiers to different individuals, groups, roles, services, or devices.

objectives.label: IA-04a.
objectives.text: system identifiers are managed by receiving authorization from {{param:ia-04_odp.01}} to assign to an individual, group, role, or device identifier;

objectives.label: IA-04b.
objectives.text: system identifiers are managed by selecting an identifier that identifies an individual, group, role, service, or device;

objectives.label: IA-04c.
objectives.text: system identifiers are managed by assigning the identifier to the intended individual, group, role, service, or device;

objectives.label: IA-04d.
objectives.text: system identifiers are managed by preventing reuse of identifiers for {{param:ia-04_odp.02}}.

parameters.label: personnel or roles
parameters.guidance: personnel or roles from whom authorization must be received to assign an identifier are defined;

parameters.guidance: a time period for preventing reuse of identifiers is defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization require authorization before assigning usernames and other identifiers, assign each to the intended person or device, and prevent reuse for a defined period?
editorial.whyItMatters: If identifiers are handed out loosely or reused, records can point to the wrong person, and a new user may inherit an old user's access or history.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Identifiers for individuals, groups, roles, services, and devices are assigned only with authorization from the personnel or roles you define. Each identifier is selected to identify its subject and assigned to the intended individual, group, role, service, or device, and identifiers are not reused for the time period you define.
nextSteps: Define who must approve new usernames and device identifiers.
Adopt a naming convention that clearly identifies each person, service, or device.

requirements.title: Prohibit Account Identifiers as Public Identifiers

statement.text: Prohibit the use of system account identifiers that are the same as public identifiers for individual accounts.

requirements.discussion: Prohibiting account identifiers as public identifiers applies to any publicly disclosed account identifier used for communication such as, electronic mail and instant messaging. Prohibiting the use of systems account identifiers that are the same as some public identifier, such as the individual identifier section of an electronic mail address, makes it more difficult for adversaries to guess user identifiers. Prohibiting account identifiers as public identifiers without the implementation of other supporting controls only complicates guessing of identifiers. Additional protections are required for authenticators and credentials to protect the account.

objectives.text: the use of system account identifiers that are the same as public identifiers is prohibited for individual accounts.

requirements.title: Identify User Status

statement.text: Manage individual identifiers by uniquely identifying each individual as {{param:ia-04.04_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Characteristics that identify the status of individuals include contractors, foreign nationals, and non-organizational users. Identifying the status of individuals by these characteristics provides additional information about the people with whom organizational personnel are communicating. For example, it might be useful for a government employee to know that one of the individuals on an email message is a contractor.

objectives.text: individual identifiers are managed by uniquely identifying each individual as {{param:ia-04.04_odp}}.

parameters.label: characteristics
parameters.guidance: characteristics used to identify individual status is defined;

editorial.question: Do your user identifiers show each person's status using characteristics your organization chooses, such as contractor, foreign national, or non-organizational user?
editorial.whyItMatters: Knowing whether someone is an employee, a contractor, or an outside user helps staff decide what information to share and with whom.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Individual identifiers are managed so that each person is uniquely identified with the status characteristics you define, such as contractor, foreign national, or non-organizational user.
nextSteps: Decide which status characteristics to show.
Add the status to usernames, display names, or email addresses in a consistent way.
