requirements.title: Dynamic Management

statement.text: Manage individual identifiers dynamically in accordance with {{param:ia-04.05_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: In contrast to conventional approaches to identification that presume static accounts for preregistered users, many distributed systems establish identifiers at runtime for entities that were previously unknown. When identifiers are established at runtime for previously unknown entities, organizations can anticipate and provision for the dynamic establishment of identifiers. Pre-established trust relationships and mechanisms with appropriate authorities to validate credentials and related identifiers are essential.

objectives.text: individual identifiers are dynamically managed in accordance with {{param:ia-04.05_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Cross-organization identifier management provides the capability to identify individuals, groups, roles, or devices when conducting cross-organization activities involving the processing, storage, or transmission of information.

requirements.title: Pairwise Pseudonymous Identifiers

statement.text: Generate pairwise pseudonymous identifiers.

requirements.discussion: A pairwise pseudonymous identifier is an opaque unguessable subscriber identifier generated by an identity provider for use at a specific individual relying party. Generating distinct pairwise pseudonymous identifiers with no identifying information about a subscriber discourages subscriber activity tracking and profiling beyond the operational requirements established by an organization. The pairwise pseudonymous identifiers are unique to each relying party except in situations where relying parties can show a demonstrable relationship justifying an operational need for correlation, or all parties consent to being correlated in such a manner.

requirements.title: Authenticator Management

statement.text: Manage system authenticators by:

items.label: a.
items.text: Verifying, as part of the initial authenticator distribution, the identity of the individual, group, role, service, or device receiving the authenticator;

items.label: b.
items.text: Establishing initial authenticator content for any authenticators issued by the organization;

items.label: c.
items.text: Ensuring that authenticators have sufficient strength of mechanism for their intended use;

items.label: d.
items.text: Establishing and implementing administrative procedures for initial authenticator distribution, for lost or compromised or damaged authenticators, and for revoking authenticators;

items.label: e.
items.text: Changing default authenticators prior to first use;

items.label: f.
items.text: Changing or refreshing authenticators {{param:ia-05_odp.01}} or when {{param:ia-05_odp.02}} occur;

items.label: g.
items.text: Protecting authenticator content from unauthorized disclosure and modification;

items.label: h.
items.text: Requiring individuals to take, and having devices implement, specific controls to protect authenticators; and

items.label: i.
items.text: Changing authenticators for group or role accounts when membership to those accounts changes.

requirements.discussion:
Authenticators include passwords, cryptographic devices, biometrics, certificates, one-time password devices, and ID badges. Device authenticators include certificates and passwords. Initial authenticator content is the actual content of the authenticator (e.g., the initial password). In contrast, the requirements for authenticator content contain specific criteria or characteristics (e.g., minimum password length). Developers may deliver system components with factory default authentication credentials (i.e., passwords) to allow for initial installation and configuration. Default authentication credentials are often well known, easily discoverable, and present a significant risk. The requirement to protect individual authenticators may be implemented via control PL-4 or PS-6 for authenticators in the possession of individuals and by controls AC-3, AC-6 , and SC-28 for authenticators stored in organizational systems, including passwords stored in hashed or encrypted formats or files containing encrypted or hashed passwords accessible with administrator privileges.

Systems support authenticator management by organization-defined settings and restrictions for various authenticator characteristics (e.g., minimum password length, validation time window for time synchronous one-time tokens, and number of allowed rejections during the verification stage of biometric authentication). Actions can be taken to safeguard individual authenticators, including maintaining possession of authenticators, not sharing authenticators with others, and immediately reporting lost, stolen, or compromised authenticators. Authenticator management includes issuing and revoking authenticators for temporary access when no longer needed.

editorial.question: Does your organization manage passwords, keys, tokens, and other authenticators securely, from issuing them through changing, replacing, and revoking them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Authenticators are what prove identity. Weak, default, shared, or poorly protected credentials let attackers impersonate legitimate users.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You verify identity before issuing an authenticator, set initial authenticator content, make sure authenticators are strong enough for their intended use, and follow procedures for initial distribution, for lost, compromised, or damaged authenticators, and for revocation. Default credentials are changed before first use, authenticators are changed or refreshed at the periods you define by type or when events you define occur, and authenticator content is protected from unauthorized disclosure and modification. Individuals and devices are required to take specific steps to protect authenticators, and authenticators for group or role accounts are changed when membership changes.
nextSteps: Change default passwords on all devices and software before putting them into use.

Store authenticators securely, for example in a password manager, and tell staff how to protect theirs.

requirements.title: Password-based Authentication

statement.text: For password-based authentication:

items.label: (a)
items.text: Maintain a list of commonly-used, expected, or compromised passwords and update the list {{param:ia-05.01_odp.01}} and when organizational passwords are suspected to have been compromised directly or indirectly;

items.label: (b)
items.text: Verify, when users create or update passwords, that the passwords are not found on the list of commonly-used, expected, or compromised passwords in IA-5(1)(a);

items.label: (c)
items.text: Transmit passwords only over cryptographically-protected channels;

items.label: (d)
items.text: Store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash;

items.label: (e)
items.text: Require immediate selection of a new password upon account recovery;

items.label: (f)
items.text: Allow user selection of long passwords and passphrases, including spaces and all printable characters;

items.label: (g)
items.text: Employ automated tools to assist the user in selecting strong password authenticators; and

items.label: (h)
items.text: Enforce the following composition and complexity rules: {{param:ia-05.01_odp.02}}.

requirements.discussion: Password-based authentication applies to passwords regardless of whether they are used in single-factor or multi-factor authentication. Long passwords or passphrases are preferable over shorter passwords. Enforced composition rules provide marginal security benefits while decreasing usability. However, organizations may choose to establish certain rules for password generation (e.g., minimum character length for long passwords) under certain circumstances and can enforce this requirement in IA-5(1)(h). Account recovery can occur, for example, in situations when a password is forgotten. Cryptographically protected passwords include salted one-way cryptographic hashes of passwords. The list of commonly used, compromised, or expected passwords includes passwords obtained from previous breach corpuses, dictionary words, and repetitive or sequential characters. The list includes context-specific words, such as the name of the service, username, and derivatives thereof.

objectives.label: IA-05(01)(a)
objectives.text: for password-based authentication, a list of commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords is maintained and updated {{param:ia-05.01_odp.01}} and when organizational passwords are suspected to have been compromised directly or indirectly;

objectives.label: IA-05(01)(h)

parameters.label: frequency
parameters.guidance: the frequency at which to update the list of commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords is defined;

parameters.label: composition and complexity rules
parameters.guidance: authenticator composition and complexity rules are defined;

editorial.question: For password logons, does your organization block common or compromised passwords, protect passwords in transit and in storage, and allow long passphrases?
editorial.whyItMatters: Attackers routinely try leaked and common passwords first. Screening them out, allowing long passphrases, and storing passwords safely reduce the chance of a successful guess and limit the damage if password files are stolen.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You maintain a list of commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords, update it at the frequency you define and when compromise is suspected, and check new or changed passwords against it. Passwords are sent only over encrypted channels, stored using an approved salted key derivation function (a one-way transformation designed to resist cracking), and must be replaced immediately after account recovery. Users can choose long passwords and passphrases with spaces and all printable characters, automated tools help them choose strong passwords, and the composition and complexity rules you define are enforced.
nextSteps: Turn on screening against breached and common passwords in your identity or directory service.
Confirm passwords are sent only over encrypted connections and stored as salted hashes.
Allow long passphrases, require a new password after account recovery, and set any composition rules you choose.

requirements.title: Public Key-based Authentication

statement.label: (a)
statement.text: For public key-based authentication:

items.text: Enforce authorized access to the corresponding private key; and
Map the authenticated identity to the account of the individual or group; and

statement.label: (b)
statement.text: When public key infrastructure (PKI) is used:

items.text: Validate certificates by constructing and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor, including checking certificate status information; and
Implement a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation.

requirements.discussion: Public key cryptography is a valid authentication mechanism for individuals, machines, and devices. For PKI solutions, status information for certification paths includes certificate revocation lists or certificate status protocol responses. For PIV cards, certificate validation involves the construction and verification of a certification path to the Common Policy Root trust anchor, which includes certificate policy processing. Implementing a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation also supports system availability in situations where organizations are unable to access revocation information via the network.

items.label: IA-05(02)(a)(01)
items.text: authorized access to the corresponding private key is enforced for public key-based authentication;

items.label: IA-05(02)(a)(02)
items.text: the authenticated identity is mapped to the account of the individual or group for public key-based authentication;

items.label: IA-05(02)(b)(01)
items.text: when public key infrastructure (PKI) is used, certificates are validated by constructing and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor, including checking certificate status information;

items.label: IA-05(02)(b)(02)
items.text: when public key infrastructure (PKI) is used, a local cache of revocation data is implemented to support path discovery and validation.

editorial.question: When people or devices sign in with certificates or other public key-based methods, does your organization protect private keys, link identities to the right accounts, and fully validate certificates?
editorial.whyItMatters: Certificate-based sign-in is strong only if private keys stay under control and certificates are checked properly. Skipping validation could let a revoked or untrusted certificate grant access.
editorial.doneLooksLike: For public key-based authentication, authorized access to the corresponding private key is enforced, and each authenticated identity is mapped to the account of the individual or group. When public key infrastructure (PKI, the system for issuing and managing certificates) is used, certificates are validated by building and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor, including checking certificate status, and a local cache of revocation data supports validation.
nextSteps: Protect private keys, for example with smart cards, hardware tokens, or PIN-protected key stores.
Configure systems to map each certificate to the correct user or group account.
Turn on full certificate path validation and revocation checking.
Set up local caching of revocation information so validation still works when the network is unavailable.

requirements.title: Change Authenticators Prior to Delivery

statement.text: Require developers and installers of system components to provide unique authenticators or change default authenticators prior to delivery and installation.

requirements.discussion: Changing authenticators prior to the delivery and installation of system components extends the requirement for organizations to change default authenticators upon system installation by requiring developers and/or installers to provide unique authenticators or change default authenticators for system components prior to delivery and/or installation. However, it typically does not apply to developers of commercial off-the-shelf information technology products. Requirements for unique authenticators can be included in acquisition documents prepared by organizations when procuring systems or system components.

objectives.text: developers and installers of system components are required to provide unique authenticators or change default authenticators prior to delivery and installation.

requirements.title: Protection of Authenticators

statement.text: Protect authenticators commensurate with the security category of the information to which use of the authenticator permits access.

requirements.discussion: For systems that contain multiple security categories of information without reliable physical or logical separation between categories, authenticators used to grant access to the systems are protected commensurate with the highest security category of information on the systems. Security categories of information are determined as part of the security categorization process.

objectives.text: authenticators are protected commensurate with the security category of the information to which use of the authenticator permits access.

editorial.question: Does your organization protect passwords, keys, tokens, and other authenticators in proportion to the sensitivity of the information they unlock?
editorial.whyItMatters: Credentials that unlock sensitive information need stronger protection, because losing one exposes everything it grants access to.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Authenticators are protected commensurate with the security category of the information they give access to. Where a system holds information of several security categories without reliable separation, authenticators are protected at the level of the highest category.
nextSteps: Identify the most sensitive information each type of authenticator can unlock.
Apply matching protection, such as encrypted storage, hardware tokens, or tighter handling rules for high-sensitivity access.
Review authenticator protection when the information a system holds becomes more sensitive.

requirements.title: No Embedded Unencrypted Static Authenticators

statement.text: Ensure that unencrypted static authenticators are not embedded in applications or other forms of static storage.

requirements.discussion: In addition to applications, other forms of static storage include access scripts and function keys. Organizations exercise caution when determining whether embedded or stored authenticators are in encrypted or unencrypted form. If authenticators are used in the manner stored, then those representations are considered unencrypted authenticators.

objectives.text: unencrypted static authenticators are not embedded in applications or other forms of static storage.

requirements.title: Multiple System Accounts

statement.text: Implement {{param:ia-05.08_odp}} to manage the risk of compromise due to individuals having accounts on multiple systems.

requirements.discussion: When individuals have accounts on multiple systems and use the same authenticators such as passwords, there is the risk that a compromise of one account may lead to the compromise of other accounts. Alternative approaches include having different authenticators (passwords) on all systems, employing a single sign-on or federation mechanism, or using some form of one-time passwords on all systems. Organizations can also use rules of behavior (see PL-4 ) and access agreements (see PS-6 ) to mitigate the risk of multiple system accounts.

objectives.text: {{param:ia-05.08_odp}} are implemented to manage the risk of compromise due to individuals having accounts on multiple systems.

statement.text: Use the following external organizations to federate credentials: {{param:ia-05.09_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Federation provides organizations with the capability to authenticate individuals and devices when conducting cross-organization activities involving the processing, storage, or transmission of information. Using a specific list of approved external organizations for authentication helps to ensure that those organizations are vetted and trusted.

requirements.title: Dynamic Credential Binding

statement.text: Bind identities and authenticators dynamically using the following rules: {{param:ia-05.10_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Authentication requires some form of binding between an identity and the authenticator that is used to confirm the identity. In conventional approaches, binding is established by pre-provisioning both the identity and the authenticator to the system. For example, the binding between a username (i.e., identity) and a password (i.e., authenticator) is accomplished by provisioning the identity and authenticator as a pair in the system. New authentication techniques allow the binding between the identity and the authenticator to be implemented external to a system. For example, with smartcard credentials, the identity and authenticator are bound together on the smartcard. Using these credentials, systems can authenticate identities that have not been pre-provisioned, dynamically provisioning the identity after authentication. In these situations, organizations can anticipate the dynamic provisioning of identities. Pre-established trust relationships and mechanisms with appropriate authorities to validate identities and related credentials are essential.

objectives.text: identities and authenticators are dynamically bound using {{param:ia-05.10_odp}}.

parameters.label: binding rules

requirements.title: Biometric Authentication Performance

statement.text: For biometric-based authentication, employ mechanisms that satisfy the following biometric quality requirements {{param:ia-05.12_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Unlike password-based authentication, which provides exact matches of user-input passwords to stored passwords, biometric authentication does not provide exact matches. Depending on the type of biometric and the type of collection mechanism, there is likely to be some divergence from the presented biometric and the stored biometric that serves as the basis for comparison. Matching performance is the rate at which a biometric algorithm correctly results in a match for a genuine user and rejects other users. Biometric performance requirements include the match rate, which reflects the accuracy of the biometric matching algorithm used by a system.

requirements.discussion: Cached authenticators are used to authenticate to the local machine when the network is not available. If cached authentication information is out of date, the validity of the authentication information may be questionable.

objectives.text: the use of cached authenticators is prohibited after {{param:ia-05.13_odp}}.

statement.text: For PKI-based authentication, employ an organization-wide methodology for managing the content of PKI trust stores installed across all platforms, including networks, operating systems, browsers, and applications.

requirements.discussion: An organization-wide methodology for managing the content of PKI trust stores helps improve the accuracy and currency of PKI-based authentication credentials across the organization.

objectives.text: an organization-wide methodology for managing the content of PKI trust stores is employed across all platforms, including networks, operating systems, browsers, and applications for PKI-based authentication.

requirements.title: GSA-approved Products and Services

statement.text: Use only General Services Administration-approved products and services for identity, credential, and access management.

requirements.discussion: General Services Administration (GSA)-approved products and services are products and services that have been approved through the GSA conformance program, where applicable, and posted to the GSA Approved Products List. GSA provides guidance for teams to design and build functional and secure systems that comply with Federal Identity, Credential, and Access Management (FICAM) policies, technologies, and implementation patterns.

requirements.title: Presentation Attack Detection for Biometric Authenticators

statement.text: Employ presentation attack detection mechanisms for biometric-based authentication.

requirements.discussion: Biometric characteristics do not constitute secrets. Such characteristics can be obtained by online web accesses, taking a picture of someone with a camera phone to obtain facial images with or without their knowledge, lifting from objects that someone has touched (e.g., a latent fingerprint), or capturing a high-resolution image (e.g., an iris pattern). Presentation attack detection technologies including liveness detection, can mitigate the risk of these types of attacks by making it difficult to produce artifacts intended to defeat the biometric sensor.

requirements.title: Password Managers

statement.label: (a)
statement.text: Employ {{param:ia-05.18_odp.01}} to generate and manage passwords; and

statement.label: (b)
statement.text: Protect the passwords using {{param:ia-05.18_odp.02}}.

requirements.discussion: For systems where static passwords are employed, it is often a challenge to ensure that the passwords are suitably complex and that the same passwords are not employed on multiple systems. A password manager is a solution to this problem as it automatically generates and stores strong and different passwords for various accounts. A potential risk of using password managers is that adversaries can target the collection of passwords generated by the password manager. Therefore, the collection of passwords requires protection including encrypting the passwords (see IA-5(1)(d) ) and storing the collection offline in a token.

objectives.text: {{param:ia-05.18_odp.01}} are employed to generate and manage passwords;

requirements.title: Authentication Feedback

statement.text: Obscure feedback of authentication information during the authentication process to protect the information from possible exploitation and use by unauthorized individuals.

requirements.discussion: Authentication feedback from systems does not provide information that would allow unauthorized individuals to compromise authentication mechanisms. For some types of systems, such as desktops or notebooks with relatively large monitors, the threat (referred to as shoulder surfing) may be significant. For other types of systems, such as mobile devices with small displays, the threat may be less significant and is balanced against the increased likelihood of typographic input errors due to small keyboards. Thus, the means for obscuring authentication feedback is selected accordingly. Obscuring authentication feedback includes displaying asterisks when users type passwords into input devices or displaying feedback for a very limited time before obscuring it.

objectives.text: the feedback of authentication information is obscured during the authentication process to protect the information from possible exploitation and use by unauthorized individuals.

editorial.question: Do your systems hide what users type during logon, for example by showing dots or asterisks instead of password characters?
editorial.whyItMatters: Passwords displayed on screen can be read by someone looking over a user's shoulder. Obscuring feedback protects credentials in shared or public spaces.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Authentication feedback is obscured during logon, for example by displaying asterisks or showing each character only briefly, using a method suited to the device, so that authentication information cannot be read and used by unauthorized individuals.
nextSteps: Check logon screens on your systems and applications to confirm password characters are masked.
Fix any custom applications that display passwords in clear text.
Review mobile device settings so that any brief display of characters fits your risk.

requirements.title: Cryptographic Module Authentication

statement.text: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines for such authentication.

requirements.discussion: Authentication mechanisms may be required within a cryptographic module to authenticate an operator accessing the module and to verify that the operator is authorized to assume the requested role and perform services within that role.

objectives.text: mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module are implemented that meet the requirements of applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines for such authentication.

editorial.question: Where your systems use cryptographic modules, do the mechanisms for authenticating to those modules meet the laws, regulations, and standards that apply to you?
editorial.whyItMatters: Cryptographic modules protect keys and perform encryption. If anyone can operate them or take on an administrative role within them, the protection they provide can be bypassed.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Mechanisms for authenticating operators to cryptographic modules, and for verifying that an operator is authorized for the requested role and services, are implemented and meet the requirements of applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines.
nextSteps: Identify the cryptographic modules your systems rely on, such as hardware security modules and built-in encryption components.
Determine which authentication requirements apply to those modules.
Configure module authentication and role assignments to meet those requirements.

requirements.title: Identification and Authentication (Non-organizational Users)

statement.text: Uniquely identify and authenticate non-organizational users or processes acting on behalf of non-organizational users.

requirements.discussion: Non-organizational users include system users other than organizational users explicitly covered by IA-2 . Non-organizational users are uniquely identified and authenticated for accesses other than those explicitly identified and documented in AC-14 . Identification and authentication of non-organizational users accessing federal systems may be required to protect federal, proprietary, or privacy-related information (with exceptions noted for national security systems). Organizations consider many factors—including security, privacy, scalability, and practicality—when balancing the need to ensure ease of use for access to federal information and systems with the need to protect and adequately mitigate risk.

objectives.text: non-organizational users or processes acting on behalf of non-organizational users are uniquely identified and authenticated.

editorial.question: Does your system uniquely identify and authenticate people outside your organization, such as customers, partners, or members of the public, who use it?
editorial.whyItMatters: Outside users can reach sensitive features and data too. Identifying each of them individually lets you control what they do and trace activity back to a specific account.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Non-organizational users, and processes acting on their behalf, are uniquely identified and authenticated, except for actions you have explicitly documented as permitted without identification or authentication.
nextSteps: List the types of outside users who access your system.
Require each to have an individual account with appropriate authentication.
Confirm any access without logon is limited to the actions you have documented as permitted.

requirements.title: Acceptance of PIV Credentials from Other Agencies

statement.text: Accept and electronically verify Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials from other federal agencies.

requirements.discussion: Acceptance of Personal Identity Verification (PIV) credentials from other federal agencies applies to both logical and physical access control systems. PIV credentials are those credentials issued by federal agencies that conform to FIPS Publication 201 and supporting guidelines. The adequacy and reliability of PIV card issuers are addressed and authorized using SP 800-79-2.

objectives.label: IA-08(01)[01]
objectives.text: Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials from other federal agencies are accepted;

objectives.label: IA-08(01)[02]
objectives.text: Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials from other federal agencies are electronically verified.

editorial.question: Do your systems accept and electronically verify Personal Identity Verification (PIV) credentials issued by other federal agencies?
editorial.whyItMatters: Federal users from other agencies already hold strong identity credentials. Accepting them avoids issuing separate, often weaker credentials and gives you a trusted way to verify who is connecting.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Credentials that conform to the PIV standard and are issued by other federal agencies are accepted by your logical and physical access control systems and electronically verified.
nextSteps: Identify users from other federal agencies who need access.
Configure systems to accept PIV credentials issued by other agencies.
Test that those credentials are electronically verified before access is granted.

requirements.title: Acceptance of External Authenticators

statement.label: (a)
statement.text: Accept only external authenticators that are NIST-compliant; and

statement.label: (b)
statement.text: Document and maintain a list of accepted external authenticators.

requirements.discussion: Acceptance of only NIST-compliant external authenticators applies to organizational systems that are accessible to the public (e.g., public-facing websites). External authenticators are issued by nonfederal government entities and are compliant with SP 800-63B . Approved external authenticators meet or exceed the minimum Federal Government-wide technical, security, privacy, and organizational maturity requirements. Meeting or exceeding Federal requirements allows Federal Government relying parties to trust external authenticators in connection with an authentication transaction at a specified authenticator assurance level.

objectives.label: IA-08(02)(a)
objectives.text: only external authenticators that are NIST-compliant are accepted;

items.label: IA-08(02)(b)[01]
items.text: a list of accepted external authenticators is documented;

items.label: IA-08(02)(b)[02]
items.text: a list of accepted external authenticators is maintained.

editorial.question: When your system accepts sign-in credentials issued by outside providers, does it accept only ones that meet NIST requirements and keep a list of them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Public-facing systems often let users sign in with credentials issued by other providers. Accepting only those that meet NIST's requirements keeps weak external credentials from undermining your system.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Only external authenticators that meet NIST's digital identity requirements are accepted, and you document and maintain a list of the external authenticators you accept.
nextSteps: Identify any external sign-in providers your public-facing systems accept.
Confirm each meets NIST's digital identity guidelines, and stop accepting those that do not.
Document the accepted providers, and keep the list current.

requirements.title: Use of Defined Profiles

statement.text: Conform to the following profiles for identity management {{param:ia-08.04_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Organizations define profiles for identity management based on open identity management standards. To ensure that open identity management standards are viable, robust, reliable, sustainable, and interoperable as documented, the Federal Government assesses and scopes the standards and technology implementations against applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines.

editorial.whyItMatters: Following defined identity profiles built on open standards lets your system work reliably with outside identity providers while applying consistent security expectations.

nextSteps: Choose the identity management profiles your system will follow.
Configure your identity federation or sign-in services to conform to those profiles.

requirements.title: Acceptance of PIV-I Credentials

statement.text: Accept and verify federated or PKI credentials that meet {{param:ia-08.05_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Acceptance of PIV-I credentials can be implemented by PIV, PIV-I, and other commercial or external identity providers. The acceptance and verification of PIV-I-compliant credentials apply to both logical and physical access control systems. The acceptance and verification of PIV-I credentials address nonfederal issuers of identity cards that desire to interoperate with United States Government PIV systems and that can be trusted by Federal Government-relying parties. The X.509 certificate policy for the Federal Bridge Certification Authority (FBCA) addresses PIV-I requirements. The PIV-I card is commensurate with the PIV credentials as defined in cited references. PIV-I credentials are the credentials issued by a PIV-I provider whose PIV-I certificate policy maps to the Federal Bridge PIV-I Certificate Policy. A PIV-I provider is cross-certified with the FBCA (directly or through another PKI bridge) with policies that have been mapped and approved as meeting the requirements of the PIV-I policies defined in the FBCA certificate policy.

requirements.title: Service Identification and Authentication

statement.text: Uniquely identify and authenticate {{param:ia-09_odp}} before establishing communications with devices, users, or other services or applications.

requirements.discussion: Services that may require identification and authentication include web applications using digital certificates or services or applications that query a database. Identification and authentication methods for system services and applications include information or code signing, provenance graphs, and electronic signatures that indicate the sources of services. Decisions regarding the validity of identification and authentication claims can be made by services separate from the services acting on those decisions. This can occur in distributed system architectures. In such situations, the identification and authentication decisions (instead of actual identifiers and authentication data) are provided to the services that need to act on those decisions.

requirements.title: Adaptive Authentication

statement.text: Require individuals accessing the system to employ {{param:ia-10_odp.01}} under specific {{param:ia-10_odp.02}}.

requirements.discussion: Adversaries may compromise individual authentication mechanisms employed by organizations and subsequently attempt to impersonate legitimate users. To address this threat, organizations may employ specific techniques or mechanisms and establish protocols to assess suspicious behavior. Suspicious behavior may include accessing information that individuals do not typically access as part of their duties, roles, or responsibilities; accessing greater quantities of information than individuals would routinely access; or attempting to access information from suspicious network addresses. When pre-established conditions or triggers occur, organizations can require individuals to provide additional authentication information. Another potential use for adaptive authentication is to increase the strength of mechanism based on the number or types of records being accessed. Adaptive authentication does not replace and is not used to avoid the use of multi-factor authentication mechanisms but can augment implementations of multi-factor authentication.

requirements.title: Re-authentication

statement.text: Require users to re-authenticate when {{param:ia-11_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: In addition to the re-authentication requirements associated with device locks, organizations may require re-authentication of individuals in certain situations, including when roles, authenticators or credentials change, when security categories of systems change, when the execution of privileged functions occurs, after a fixed time period, or periodically.

requirements.title: Identity Proofing

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Identity proof users that require accounts for logical access to systems based on appropriate identity assurance level requirements as specified in applicable standards and guidelines;

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Resolve user identities to a unique individual; and

statement.label: c.
statement.text: Collect, validate, and verify identity evidence.

requirements.discussion: Identity proofing is the process of collecting, validating, and verifying a user’s identity information for the purposes of establishing credentials for accessing a system. Identity proofing is intended to mitigate threats to the registration of users and the establishment of their accounts. Standards and guidelines specifying identity assurance levels for identity proofing include SP 800-63-3 and SP 800-63A . Organizations may be subject to laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, or policies that address the collection of identity evidence. Organizational personnel consult with the senior agency official for privacy and legal counsel regarding such requirements.

objectives.text: users who require accounts for logical access to systems based on appropriate identity assurance level requirements as specified in applicable standards and guidelines are identity proofed;

editorial.question: Before giving people accounts, does your organization confirm their identity to the required assurance level by collecting and checking evidence that they are who they claim to be?
editorial.whyItMatters: If someone can register under a false name, your other access controls end up protecting the wrong person. Identity proofing makes sure accounts go to real, correctly identified people.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Users who need accounts for logical access are identity proofed at the identity assurance level required by applicable standards and guidelines, such as NIST SP 800-63A. Each identity is resolved to a unique individual, and identity evidence is collected, validated, and verified.
nextSteps: Determine the identity assurance level each system requires, using NIST digital identity guidelines.
Define what identity evidence you collect and how you validate and verify it.
Confirm each identity maps to one unique person before an account is created.
Consult privacy and legal advisors on rules that apply to collecting identity evidence.

requirements.title: Supervisor Authorization

statement.text: Require that the registration process to receive an account for logical access includes supervisor or sponsor authorization.

requirements.discussion: Including supervisor or sponsor authorization as part of the registration process provides an additional level of scrutiny to ensure that the user’s management chain is aware of the account, the account is essential to carry out organizational missions and functions, and the user’s privileges are appropriate for the anticipated responsibilities and authorities within the organization.

objectives.text: the registration process to receive an account for logical access includes supervisor or sponsor authorization.

requirements.title: Identity Evidence

statement.text: Require evidence of individual identification be presented to the registration authority.

requirements.discussion: Identity evidence, such as documentary evidence or a combination of documents and biometrics, reduces the likelihood of individuals using fraudulent identification to establish an identity or at least increases the work factor of potential adversaries. The forms of acceptable evidence are consistent with the risks to the systems, roles, and privileges associated with the user’s account.

objectives.text: evidence of individual identification is presented to the registration authority.

editorial.question: Does your organization require people to present evidence of their identity, such as identity documents, to the person or office responsible for registering users?
editorial.whyItMatters: Requiring evidence makes it much harder for someone to set up an account under a false or borrowed identity.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Evidence of individual identification, such as documents or a combination of documents and biometrics, is presented to the registration authority. The forms of evidence you accept match the risks of the system, role, and privileges involved.
nextSteps: Designate the registration authority that receives identity evidence.
Define the acceptable forms of evidence for each type of account, based on risk.
Record that evidence was presented before accounts are issued.

requirements.title: Identity Evidence Validation and Verification

statement.text: Require that the presented identity evidence be validated and verified through {{param:ia-12.03_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Validation and verification of identity evidence increases the assurance that accounts and identifiers are being established for the correct user and authenticators are being bound to that user. Validation refers to the process of confirming that the evidence is genuine and authentic, and the data contained in the evidence is correct, current, and related to an individual. Verification confirms and establishes a linkage between the claimed identity and the actual existence of the user presenting the evidence. Acceptable methods for validating and verifying identity evidence are consistent with the risks to the systems, roles, and privileges associated with the users account.

objectives.text: the presented identity evidence is validated and verified through {{param:ia-12.03_odp}}.

parameters.label: methods of validation and verification
parameters.guidance: methods of validation and verification of identity evidence are defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization check that presented identity evidence is genuine and belongs to the person presenting it, using validation and verification methods it defines?
editorial.whyItMatters: A forged or borrowed document can pass a quick glance. Validating the evidence and verifying the person matches it makes sure accounts go to the right person.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Presented identity evidence is validated, confirming it is genuine and its details are correct and current, and verified, confirming it links to the actual person presenting it. The methods used are the ones you define, matched to the risks of the account.
nextSteps: Define how you will check that evidence is genuine, such as examining security features or confirming details with the issuing source.
Define how you will confirm the person matches the evidence, such as comparing a photo.
Document the methods, and train registration staff to apply them.

requirements.title: In-person Validation and Verification

statement.text: Require that the validation and verification of identity evidence be conducted in person before a designated registration authority.

requirements.discussion: In-person proofing reduces the likelihood of fraudulent credentials being issued because it requires the physical presence of individuals, the presentation of physical identity documents, and actual face-to-face interactions with designated registration authorities.

objectives.text: the validation and verification of identity evidence is conducted in person before a designated registration authority.

editorial.question: Does your organization require identity evidence to be validated and verified in person, before a designated registration authority?
editorial.whyItMatters: Face-to-face proofing requires the person to appear with physical documents, which makes fraudulent registration much harder.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Validation and verification of identity evidence are conducted in person before a designated registration authority, with the individual physically present and presenting physical identity documents.
nextSteps: Designate the registration authorities who will conduct in-person proofing.
Write a procedure for in-person sessions, including which documents are checked and how results are recorded.
Arrange in-person options for staff at other locations.

requirements.title: Address Confirmation

statement.text: Require that a {{param:ia-12.05_odp}} be delivered through an out-of-band channel to verify the users address (physical or digital) of record.

requirements.discussion: To make it more difficult for adversaries to pose as legitimate users during the identity proofing process, organizations can use out-of-band methods to ensure that the individual associated with an address of record is the same individual that participated in the registration. Confirmation can take the form of a temporary enrollment code or a notice of proofing. The delivery address for these artifacts is obtained from records and not self-asserted by the user. The address can include a physical or digital address. A home address is an example of a physical address. Email addresses and telephone numbers are examples of digital addresses.

objectives.text: a {{param:ia-12.05_odp}} is delivered through an out-of-band channel to verify the user’s address (physical or digital) of record.

editorial.question: Does your organization confirm a new user's address of record by sending a registration code or notice of proofing through a separate, out-of-band channel?
editorial.whyItMatters: Sending confirmation through a different channel, to an address taken from your records rather than one the applicant supplies, makes it harder for an impostor to complete registration.
editorial.doneLooksLike: A registration code or notice of proofing, as you have selected, is delivered through an out-of-band channel (a communication path separate from the registration itself) to verify the user's physical or digital address of record. The address comes from records rather than from the user's own claim.
nextSteps: Choose whether to send a registration code or a notice of proofing.
Obtain the delivery address, such as a mailing address, email address, or phone number, from existing records.
Send it through a channel separate from the registration session, and track that delivery occurred.

requirements.title: Accept Externally-proofed Identities

statement.text: Accept externally-proofed identities at {{param:ia-12.06_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: To limit unnecessary re-proofing of identities, particularly of non-PIV users, organizations accept proofing conducted at a commensurate level of assurance by other agencies or organizations. Proofing is consistent with organizational security policy and the identity assurance level appropriate for the system, application, or information accessed. Accepting externally-proofed identities is a fundamental component of managing federated identities across agencies and organizations.

objectives.text: externally proofed identities are accepted {{param:ia-12.06_odp}}.

parameters.label: identity assurance level

requirements.title: Identity Providers and Authorization Servers

statement.text: Employ identity providers and authorization servers to manage user, device, and non-person entity (NPE) identities, attributes, and access rights supporting authentication and authorization decisions in accordance with {{param:ia-13_odp.01}} using {{param:ia-13_odp.02}}.

requirements.discussion: Identity providers, both internal and external to the organization, manage the user, device, and NPE authenticators and issue statements, often called identity assertions, attesting to identities of other systems or systems components. Authorization servers create and issue access tokens to identified and authenticated users and devices that can be used to gain access to system or information resources. For example, single sign-on (SSO) provides identity provider and authorization server functions. Authenticator management (to include credential management) is covered by IA-05.

statement.text: Cryptographic keys that protect access tokens are generated, managed, and protected from disclosure and misuse.

requirements.discussion: Identity assertions and access tokens are typically digitally signed. The private keys used to sign these assertions and tokens are protected commensurate with the impact of the system and information resources that can be accessed.

requirements.title: Verification of Identity Assertions and Access Tokens

statement.text: The source and integrity of identity assertions and access tokens are verified before granting access to system and information resources.

requirements.discussion: This includes verification of digital signatures protecting identity assertions and access tokens, as well as included metadata. Metadata includes information about the access request such as information unique to user, system or information resource being accessed, or the transaction itself such as time. Protected system and information resources could include connected networks, applications, and APIs.

statement.text: In accordance with {{param:ia-13_odp.01}}, assertions and access tokens are:

requirements.discussion: An access token is a piece of data that represents the authorization granted to a user or NPE to access specific systems or information resources. Access tokens enable controlled access to services and resources. Properly managing the lifecycle of access tokens, including their issuance, validation, and revocation, is crucial to maintaining confidentiality of data and systems. Restricting token validity to a specific audience, e.g., an application or security domain, and restricting token validity lifetimes are important practices. Access tokens are revoked or invalidated if they are compromised, lost, or are no longer needed to mitigate the risks associated with stolen or misused tokens.

requirements.title: Policy and Procedures

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Develop, document, and disseminate to {{param:ir-1_prm_1}}:

items.text: {{param:ir-01_odp.03}} incident response policy that:

items.label: (a)
items.text: Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and

items.label: (b)
items.text: Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the incident response policy and the associated incident response controls;

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Designate an {{param:ir-01_odp.04}} to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the incident response policy and procedures; and

Procedures {{param:ir-01_odp.07}} and following {{param:ir-01_odp.08}}.

requirements.discussion: Incident response policy and procedures address the controls in the IR family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance. Therefore, it is important that security and privacy programs collaborate on the development of incident response policy and procedures. Security and privacy program policies and procedures at the organization level are preferable, in general, and may obviate the need for mission- or system-specific policies and procedures. The policy can be included as part of the general security and privacy policy or be represented by multiple policies that reflect the complex nature of organizations. Procedures can be established for security and privacy programs, for mission or business processes, and for systems, if needed. Procedures describe how the policies or controls are implemented and can be directed at the individual or role that is the object of the procedure. Procedures can be documented in system security and privacy plans or in one or more separate documents. Events that may precipitate an update to incident response policy and procedures include assessment or audit findings, security incidents or breaches, or changes in laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Simply restating controls does not constitute an organizational policy or procedure.

editorial.question: Does your organization have a documented incident response policy and procedures that are shared with the right people, owned by a named official, and reviewed on a set schedule?
editorial.whyItMatters: When something goes wrong, people fall back on what is written down and what they were told. A clear policy sets who is responsible for responding to incidents, and procedures turn it into steps people can follow under pressure.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have a written incident response policy that covers purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination across teams, and compliance, is consistent with the laws and regulations that apply to you, and is backed by procedures for carrying it out. Both are distributed to the people or roles you designate and managed by an official you name. You review and update each at the frequency you set and after the events you define, such as a security incident, an audit finding, or a change in law.
nextSteps: Name the official who owns the incident response policy and procedures.

requirements.title: Incident Response Training

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Provide incident response training to system users consistent with assigned roles and responsibilities:

items.text: Within {{param:ir-02_odp.01}} of assuming an incident response role or responsibility or acquiring system access;
When required by system changes; and
{{param:ir-02_odp.02}} thereafter; and

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Review and update incident response training content {{param:ir-02_odp.03}} and following {{param:ir-02_odp.04}}.

requirements.discussion: Incident response training is associated with the assigned roles and responsibilities of organizational personnel to ensure that the appropriate content and level of detail are included in such training. For example, users may only need to know who to call or how to recognize an incident; system administrators may require additional training on how to handle incidents; and incident responders may receive more specific training on forensics, data collection techniques, reporting, system recovery, and system restoration. Incident response training includes user training in identifying and reporting suspicious activities from external and internal sources. Incident response training for users may be provided as part of AT-2 or AT-3 . Events that may precipitate an update to incident response training content include, but are not limited to, incident response plan testing or response to an actual incident (lessons learned), assessment or audit findings, or changes in applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

editorial.question: Do people receive incident response training suited to their role when they start, when systems change, and on a regular schedule after that?
editorial.whyItMatters: Most incidents are first noticed by ordinary users and then handled by a few people under time pressure. Role-based training means everyone knows how to spot and report a problem, and responders know what to do next.
editorial.doneLooksLike: System users receive incident response training matched to their role within a time period you set after gaining system access or taking on an incident response role, when system changes require it, and at a frequency you define after that. For example, general users learn to recognize and report suspicious activity, while administrators and responders learn handling and recovery steps. You review and update the training content at a frequency you set and after events you define, such as lessons learned from an incident or a plan test.
nextSteps: Identify the roles that need incident response training and what each one needs to know.
Set the deadline for initial training after someone gains access or takes on a response role, and the refresher frequency.
Add significant system changes as a trigger for additional training.
Schedule reviews of the training content, including after incidents and plan tests.

requirements.title: Simulated Events

statement.text: Incorporate simulated events into incident response training to facilitate the required response by personnel in crisis situations.

requirements.discussion: Organizations establish requirements for responding to incidents in incident response plans. Incorporating simulated events into incident response training helps to ensure that personnel understand their individual responsibilities and what specific actions to take in crisis situations.

objectives.text: simulated events are incorporated into incident response training to facilitate the required response by personnel in crisis situations.

editorial.question: Does your incident response training include simulated events, such as mock incidents or scenario drills, so people practice the actions they would take in a real crisis?
editorial.whyItMatters: Knowing a procedure on paper is different from carrying it out under pressure. Practicing with realistic scenarios helps people remember their own role and respond quickly when a real incident happens.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Your incident response training incorporates simulated events, such as a staged phishing compromise or a mock ransomware outbreak, that require participants to carry out the response your incident response plan expects of them. Participants can describe their individual responsibilities and the specific actions they would take.
nextSteps: Pick two or three realistic incident scenarios drawn from your incident response plan.
Build each scenario into training so participants make decisions and take actions rather than only listen.
Note where people were unsure of their role and update the training or plan to address it.

requirements.discussion: Automated mechanisms can provide a more thorough and realistic incident response training environment. This can be accomplished, for example, by providing more complete coverage of incident response issues, selecting more realistic training scenarios and environments, and stressing the response capability.

editorial.whyItMatters: Automated training environments can recreate realistic systems, alerts, and attack activity that are hard to stage by hand. They let responders practice more scenarios and test how well the team holds up under load without touching production systems.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have identified the automated mechanisms you use for incident response training, such as a simulation platform, a cyber range, or a lab that generates realistic alerts and system behavior, and responders train in that environment.
nextSteps: Decide which automated tools will provide your incident response training environment.

requirements.title: Breach

statement.text: Provide incident response training on how to identify and respond to a breach, including the organization’s process for reporting a breach.

requirements.discussion: For federal agencies, an incident that involves personally identifiable information is considered a breach. A breach results in the loss of control, compromise, unauthorized disclosure, unauthorized acquisition, or a similar occurrence where a person other than an authorized user accesses or potentially accesses personally identifiable information or an authorized user accesses or potentially accesses such information for other than authorized purposes. The incident response training emphasizes the obligation of individuals to report both confirmed and suspected breaches involving information in any medium or form, including paper, oral, and electronic. Incident response training includes tabletop exercises that simulate a breach. See IR-2(1).

objectives.label: IR-02(03)[01]
objectives.text: incident response training on how to identify and respond to a breach is provided;

objectives.label: IR-02(03)[02]
objectives.text: incident response training on the organization’s process for reporting a breach is provided.

editorial.question: Does your incident response training teach people how to recognize and respond to a breach of personal information, and how to report one through your process?
editorial.whyItMatters: A breach of personally identifiable information (information that can identify a person) can harm the people affected and may carry legal notice duties. Staff who know what a breach looks like and where to report it, even when only suspected, give your organization time to respond properly.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Your incident response training covers how to identify a breach involving personally identifiable information in any form, including paper, spoken, and electronic, and how to respond to it. It also explains your organization's process for reporting breaches and stresses that both confirmed and suspected breaches must be reported.
nextSteps: Add a breach module to incident response training that explains what counts as a breach, with examples for paper, spoken, and electronic information.
Explain the reporting process step by step, including who to contact and how quickly.
Include a tabletop exercise that simulates a breach.

requirements.title: Incident Response Testing

statement.text: Test the effectiveness of the incident response capability for the system {{param:ir-03_odp.01}} using the following tests: {{param:ir-03_odp.02}}.

requirements.discussion: Organizations test incident response capabilities to determine their effectiveness and identify potential weaknesses or deficiencies. Incident response testing includes the use of checklists, walk-through or tabletop exercises, and simulations (parallel or full interrupt). Incident response testing can include a determination of the effects on organizational operations and assets and individuals due to incident response. The use of qualitative and quantitative data aids in determining the effectiveness of incident response processes.

objectives.text: the effectiveness of the incident response capability for the system is tested {{param:ir-03_odp.01}} using {{param:ir-03_odp.02}}.

parameters.label: frequency

parameters.guidance: tests used to test the effectiveness of the incident response capability for the system are defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization test how well its incident response capability works, using the types of tests and at the frequency you have defined?
editorial.whyItMatters: An incident response plan that has never been tested often fails at the first real use, because contact details are stale, steps are unclear, or tools do not work as expected. Testing finds these weaknesses while the stakes are low.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have defined how often the incident response capability for the system is tested and which tests are used, such as checklists, walk-throughs, tabletop exercises, or simulations. Tests are carried out on that schedule and the results are recorded, along with weaknesses found and how they were addressed.
nextSteps: Decide which types of incident response tests you will use and how often you will run them.

requirements.title: Incident Handling

statement.label: a.
statement.text: Implement an incident handling capability for incidents that is consistent with the incident response plan and includes preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery;

statement.label: b.
statement.text: Coordinate incident handling activities with contingency planning activities;

statement.text: Ensure the rigor, intensity, scope, and results of incident handling activities are comparable and predictable across the organization.

requirements.discussion: Organizations recognize that incident response capabilities are dependent on the capabilities of organizational systems and the mission and business processes being supported by those systems. Organizations consider incident response as part of the definition, design, and development of mission and business processes and systems. Incident-related information can be obtained from a variety of sources, including audit monitoring, physical access monitoring, and network monitoring; user or administrator reports; and reported supply chain events. An effective incident handling capability includes coordination among many organizational entities (e.g., mission or business owners, system owners, authorizing officials, human resources offices, physical security offices, personnel security offices, legal departments, risk executive [function], operations personnel, procurement offices). Suspected security incidents include the receipt of suspicious email communications that can contain malicious code. Suspected supply chain incidents include the insertion of counterfeit hardware or malicious code into organizational systems or system components. For federal agencies, an incident that involves personally identifiable information is considered a breach. A breach results in unauthorized disclosure, the loss of control, unauthorized acquisition, compromise, or a similar occurrence where a person other than an authorized user accesses or potentially accesses personally identifiable information or an authorized user accesses or potentially accesses such information for other than authorized purposes.

editorial.question: Does your organization have a working way to prepare for, detect, analyze, contain, remove, and recover from security incidents that follows its incident response plan?
editorial.whyItMatters: Without a defined handling process, incidents tend to be discovered late, contained inconsistently, and repeated. A consistent capability limits damage and shortens recovery.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Your incident handling follows your incident response plan and covers preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication (removing the cause), and recovery. Handling is coordinated with your contingency planning, lessons learned are fed into procedures, training, and testing and the resulting changes are made, and incidents are handled with comparable rigor, intensity, scope, and results across the organization.
nextSteps: Write down the steps for each phase: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery.
Link incident handling to your contingency or business continuity plans so recovery steps match.
Hold a short lessons-learned review after each significant incident and track the resulting changes to completion.
Use a common checklist or template so every incident is handled to the same standard.

editorial.doneLooksLike: You have identified the automated mechanisms that support your incident handling process, such as an online incident management system or tools for collecting live response data, capturing network traffic, and performing forensic analysis, and responders use them during incidents.
nextSteps: Decide which incident handling steps would benefit most from automation, such as tracking, evidence collection, or analysis.

requirements.title: Integrated Incident Response Team

statement.text: Establish and maintain an integrated incident response team that can be deployed to any location identified by the organization in {{param:ir-04.11_odp}}.

requirements.discussion:
An integrated incident response team is a team of experts that assesses, documents, and responds to incidents so that organizational systems and networks can recover quickly and implement the necessary controls to avoid future incidents. Incident response team personnel include forensic and malicious code analysts, tool developers, systems security and privacy engineers, and real-time operations personnel. The incident handling capability includes performing rapid forensic preservation of evidence and analysis of and response to intrusions. For some organizations, the incident response team can be a cross-organizational entity.

An integrated incident response team facilitates information sharing and allows organizational personnel (e.g., developers, implementers, and operators) to leverage team knowledge of the threat and implement defensive measures that enable organizations to deter intrusions more effectively. Moreover, integrated teams promote the rapid detection of intrusions, the development of appropriate mitigations, and the deployment of effective defensive measures. For example, when an intrusion is detected, the integrated team can rapidly develop an appropriate response for operators to implement, correlate the new incident with information on past intrusions, and augment ongoing cyber intelligence development. Integrated incident response teams are better able to identify adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures that are linked to the operations tempo or specific mission and business functions and to define responsive actions in a way that does not disrupt those mission and business functions. Incident response teams can be distributed within organizations to make the capability resilient.

The team can deploy to any location your organization identifies within the time period you define, and that ability has been confirmed, for example through exercises.

requirements.title: Security Operations Center

statement.text: Establish and maintain a security operations center.

requirements.discussion: A security operations center (SOC) is the focal point for security operations and computer network defense for an organization. The purpose of the SOC is to defend and monitor an organization’s systems and networks (i.e., cyber infrastructure) on an ongoing basis. The SOC is also responsible for detecting, analyzing, and responding to cybersecurity incidents in a timely manner. The organization staffs the SOC with skilled technical and operational personnel (e.g., security analysts, incident response personnel, systems security engineers) and implements a combination of technical, management, and operational controls (including monitoring, scanning, and forensics tools) to monitor, fuse, correlate, analyze, and respond to threat and security-relevant event data from multiple sources. These sources include perimeter defenses, network devices (e.g., routers, switches), and endpoint agent data feeds. The SOC provides a holistic situational awareness capability to help organizations determine the security posture of the system and organization. A SOC capability can be obtained in a variety of ways. Larger organizations may implement a dedicated SOC while smaller organizations may employ third-party organizations to provide such a capability.

requirements.title: Supply Chain Coordination

statement.text: Provide incident information to the provider of the product or service and other organizations involved in the supply chain or supply chain governance for systems or system components related to the incident.

requirements.discussion: Organizations involved in supply chain activities include product developers, system integrators, manufacturers, packagers, assemblers, distributors, vendors, and resellers. Entities that provide supply chain governance include the Federal Acquisition Security Council (FASC). Supply chain incidents include compromises or breaches that involve information technology products, system components, development processes or personnel, distribution processes, or warehousing facilities. Organizations determine the appropriate information to share and consider the value gained from informing external organizations about supply chain incidents, including the ability to improve processes or to identify the root cause of an incident.

objectives.text: incident information is provided to the provider of the product or service and other organizations involved in the supply chain or supply chain governance for systems or system components related to the incident.

editorial.question: When an incident involves a product or service you obtained from a supplier, does your organization share relevant incident information with that provider and others in the supply chain?
editorial.whyItMatters: A compromised product or service often affects other customers too, and the provider may be the only party able to find and fix the root cause. Sharing information helps stop the problem from spreading and improves the product.
editorial.doneLooksLike: For incidents related to a system or component you obtained externally, incident information is provided to the product or service provider and to other organizations involved in the supply chain or supply chain governance. You decide what information is appropriate to share in each case.
nextSteps: Add a step to your incident handling procedure to identify whether a supplier's product or service was involved.
Keep current security contact details for your key suppliers.
Define what incident information may be shared with suppliers and who approves sharing it.

requirements.title: Incident Response Assistance

statement.text: Provide an incident response support resource, integral to the organizational incident response capability, that offers advice and assistance to users of the system for the handling and reporting of incidents.

requirements.discussion: Incident response support resources provided by organizations include help desks, assistance groups, automated ticketing systems to open and track incident response tickets, and access to forensics services or consumer redress services, when required.

objectives.label: IR-07[01]
objectives.text: an incident response support resource, integral to the organizational incident response capability, is provided;

objectives.label: IR-07[02]
objectives.text: the incident response support resource offers advice and assistance to users of the system for the response and reporting of incidents.

editorial.question: Is there a support resource, such as a help desk or designated contact, that people can turn to for advice on handling and reporting incidents?
editorial.whyItMatters: People who suspect a problem often hesitate because they are unsure whom to ask or whether it matters. An available support resource gets incidents reported sooner and handled correctly.
editorial.doneLooksLike: A support resource that is part of your incident response capability, such as a help desk, a designated responder, a ticketing channel, or access to outside forensic services, is available to system users and offers advice and assistance on handling and reporting incidents.
nextSteps: Designate the help desk, person, or service that users should contact about a suspected incident.
Publish the contact details where users will find them, such as onboarding material and the staff intranet.
Arrange outside incident response or forensic support in advance if you lack that expertise in-house.

requirements.title: Automation Support for Availability of Information and Support

statement.text: Increase the availability of incident response information and support using {{param:ir-07.01_odp}}.

requirements.discussion: Automated mechanisms can provide a push or pull capability for users to obtain incident response assistance. For example, individuals may have access to a website to query the assistance capability, or the assistance capability can proactively send incident response information to users (general distribution or targeted) as part of increasing understanding of current response capabilities and support.

objectives.text: the availability of incident response information and support is increased using {{param:ir-07.01_odp}}.

parameters.label: automated mechanisms
parameters.guidance: automated mechanisms used to increase the availability of incident response information and support are defined;

editorial.question: Does your organization use automated mechanisms, such as a help portal or automatic notices, to make incident response information and support more available to users?
editorial.whyItMatters: People are more likely to report problems and follow the right steps when help is quick to find. Automated access to guidance and support shortens the time between noticing an issue and acting on it.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have defined the automated mechanisms used to increase the availability of incident response information and support, such as a website users can search for guidance, or notices that are sent to users about current response capabilities, and users can reach them when needed.
nextSteps: Decide how users will find incident response help, such as an internal web page or service desk portal.
Publish clear guidance there on how to report incidents and get assistance.
Consider sending targeted notices to users when a current threat or response step affects them.
